summary: Parallel domain research on CSAM-prevention + porn-addiction-harm orgs/researchers/competitors, then synthesize a gap analysis + content backlog vs the existing site

entities.name: National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC)
entities.covers: US nonprofit (est. 1984) operating the CyberTipline — the legally mandated US reporting channel for online child sexual exploitation; US electronic service providers (ESPs) must report apparent CSAM to it under 18 U.S.C. 2258A. Also runs Take It Down, the Child Victim Identification Program (CVIP), and 1-800-THE-LOST.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS (cite with year): The CyberTipline received 20.5 million reports of suspected child sexual exploitation in 2024 (down from a record 36.2 million in 2023 — the drop is largely an artifact of a new 2024 'bundling' feature Meta adopted that consolidates viral-meme reports; adjusted for incidents the 2024 figure is ~29.2 million distinct incidents). 2024 reports contained 62.9 million files (33.1M videos, 28M images, ~2M other). 84% of 2024 reports resolved OUTSIDE the US. Generative-AI reports surged 1,325%, from 4,700 (2023) to 67,000 (2024). Online enticement (incl. sextortion) reports rose ~192%, from 186,000 (2023) to 546,000+ (2024) — partly due to the REPORT Act (signed May 2024) mandating enticement/trafficking reporting. The CyberTipline also received 164,497 public reports in 2024. NEWER (NCMEC '2025 first look,' pub. 2026): 21.3 million reports in 2025; 1.4 million online-enticement reports (+158% vs 2024); child sex trafficking 113,500+ reports (+323%); NCMEC referred 18.8M+ reports to law enforcement; 61.8M files (29.4M images, 26.3M videos, 6.1M other); 158,000 files categorized as GAI CSAM since 2023. CRITICAL ACCURACY NUANCE (Stanford/Riana Pfefferkorn, cyberlaw.stanford.edu, 2025-26): a CyberTipline report flagged 'Generative AI' does NOT necessarily mean the file IS AI-generated CSAM — the category is ambiguous; press coverage conflating Amazon's ~380,000 GAI-flagged H1-2025 reports with 'hundreds of thousands of pieces of AI CSAM' was misleading. PROGRAMS TO LINK: report at report.cybertip.org; Take It Down (takeitdown.ncmec.org), launched Feb 27 2023 with Meta as founding partner, lets a minor (or adult who was a minor in the image) hash a nude/explicit image ON-DEVICE — only the hash, never the image, is sent to NCMEC — and participating platforms detect/block matches; 1-800-843-5678 (1-800-THE-LOST).

entities.name: Internet Watch Foundation (IWF)
entities.covers: UK charity and hotline (est. 1996) that finds, assesses, and removes CSAM worldwide via notice-and-takedown and produces widely cited threat-intelligence. Licenses hash lists, URL lists, keyword lists, and classifiers to industry; with NSPCC runs Report Remove.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS (IWF Annual Data & Insights Report 2024, pub. Jan 2025): IWF actioned a record 291,270 webpages of confirmed CSAM in 2024 (+5% vs 275,650 in 2023) — the most in its 29-year history; each webpage can hold one to thousands of images/videos; 1,228,090 webpages removed over the past 5 years. In 2024 analysts assessed a report every 74 seconds; every 108 seconds a report showed a child being sexually abused. The EU now hosts more than half of global CSAM webpages IWF finds; the Netherlands is the single most-abused hosting location. AI-CSAM (VERIFIED): IWF actioned 245 reports containing AI-generated CSAM in 2024 (+380% vs 51 in 2023), totaling 7,644 images plus a small number of videos; 7,063 of those items were realistic enough to be treated as 'real' under UK law; 98% (6,945) depicted girls; IWF confirmed its FIRST realistic AI-generated CSAM VIDEOS in 2024 (9 deepfake videos found on one dark-web forum in a March–April 2024 snapshot). Landmark research: 'How AI is being abused to create child sexual abuse imagery' (Oct 2023) found 20,000+ AI images on one dark-web forum in a month, 11,108 assessed, 2,562 confirmed criminal; a 2024 follow-up found 12,000+ new AI images on a dark-web forum in a month (90% realistic enough to be assessed as real CSAM, 3,500+ confirmed criminal). Older, unfiltered versions of Stable Diffusion are 'overwhelmingly the software of choice'; offenders fine-tune models to generate known victims on demand. 'Self-generated' imagery (a term IWF popularized) dominates; per IWF data cited by WeProtect, self-generated imagery of 7–10-year-olds rose 360% from 2020 to 2022. Tools: IntelliGrade, Image Hash List, URL List, Keywords List, CSAM classifier; parent checklist 'TALK.'

entities.name: Thorn
entities.covers: US nonprofit (founded 2012 by Demi Moore and Ashton Kutcher) building technology to defend children from sexual abuse. Flagship product Safer (safer.io) provides CSAM hash-matching and ML classifiers to platforms; also runs research and the NoFiltr / Thorn for Parents education programs.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS (Safer 2024 Impact Report): in 2024 Safer detected 1,979,406 known CSAM files via hash matching and 2,237,225 potential NOVEL CSAM files via predictive AI classifiers — 4,162,256 suspected CSAM files total; processed 112.3 billion files in 2024; 60+ platforms in the community; cumulatively (since 2019) Safer has processed 228.8 billion files and detected 6,475,553 CSAM files. In July 2024 Thorn launched Safer Predict (AI classifiers for image/video AND line-by-line text to flag sextortion/grooming). FRAMEWORK TO CITE: Thorn co-authored, with All Tech Is Human, 'Safety by Design for Generative AI: Preventing Child Sexual Abuse' (April 2024), with Develop/Deploy/Maintain commitments signed by Amazon, Anthropic, Civitai, Google, Meta, Metaphysic, Microsoft, Mistral AI, OpenAI, Stability AI (Invoke joined July 2024). Thorn's first Annual Progress Report (April 2024–April 2025, pub. 2025) tracked implementation — signatories reported detecting/blocking hundreds of thousands of harmful-generation attempts and removing hundreds of models built to create child-abuse imagery. This is the single most citable industry standard for AI labs on child safety. Youth/parent brands: NoFiltr (nofiltr.org), Thorn for Parents. (Historical: Thorn formerly built Spotlight to help law enforcement find child-trafficking victims in escort ads.)

entities.name: Technology Coalition (Tech Coalition) — Lantern
entities.covers: Nonprofit industry alliance (founded 2006, reconstituted 2020 under 'Project Protect') coordinating the tech sector against online child sexual exploitation and abuse (OCSEA). Members include Google, Meta, Microsoft, Apple, Amazon, Discord, Snap, Roblox, and many others. Runs Lantern, the first cross-platform signal-sharing program for child safety.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED FACTS: Lantern launched November 2023 as the first cross-platform signal-sharing program; participating companies securely share signals — hashes of known violating content, CSE-related keywords, and URLs — so an offender pushed off one platform can be detected when they move to another (solving the gap where each platform only saw its own slice of offender behavior). Initial participants: Discord, Google, Mega, Meta, Quora, Roblox, Snap, Twitch; Lantern is hosted on Meta's ThreatExchange and has since expanded toward the financial sector (e.g., Block joined). The Tech Coalition co-funds, with Safe Online (End Violence Partnership), the multi-million-dollar Safe Online Research Fund to expand the OCSEA evidence base, publishes annual transparency/impact reports plus a voluntary industry-transparency framework, and runs working groups on sextortion, grooming, and generative AI. Best single citation for HOW platforms cooperate and for the cross-platform-offender problem.

entities.name: WeProtect Global Alliance
entities.covers: Global multistakeholder alliance (governments across ~100+ countries, plus companies and civil society; formed by merging the UK-initiated WePROTECT and the US-initiated Global Alliance Against Child Sexual Abuse Online) driving a coordinated international response to OCSEA.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: TWO CITABLE ASSETS. (1) The biennial 'Global Threat Assessment' (editions 2018, 2019, 2021, 2023; a 2025 edition exists — check key-findings page). VERIFIED 2023 headline stats: reports of CSAM increased 87% since 2019 (NCMEC), with 32M+ reports globally in 2022; self-generated sexual imagery of 7–10-year-olds rose 360% from 2020 to 2022 (IWF); online grooming on social-gaming platforms can escalate to high-risk in as little as 19 seconds, with an average grooming time of ~45 minutes (Crisp, 2023); financially motivated sextortion of teenage boys and generative-AI CSAM identified as emerging threats (the report noted <1% of files in offender communities were then photorealistic CGI — a baseline now rising fast). (2) The 'Model National Response' (MNR) — the standard framework of capabilities every country should have across Policy & Governance, Criminal Justice, Victim, and Societal dimensions; governments self-assess against it. Best citation for international policy and 'what good national capability looks like.'

entities.name: INHOPE (International Association of Internet Hotlines)
entities.covers: Global network coordinating CSAM reporting hotlines, enabling cross-border notice-and-takedown. Operates ICCAM, the secure hash-based platform hotlines use to exchange/de-duplicate reports and connect to INTERPOL's ICSE database.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS: In 2024 the network comprised 55 hotlines across 51 countries (the broader directory lists 67 hotlines; new 2024 members included ACSAI in Nigeria and the Internet Hotline Centre in Japan) and processed nearly 2.5 million records of suspected CSAM via ICCAM — a 218% increase over 2023; 65% of records contained illegal content and 37% was new content needing further assessment; CSAM was traced to 86 countries; 93% of victims were children aged 3–13 and 99% were girls. CRITICAL SPEED STAT: response time to remove content was 1.4 days WITHIN the INHOPE network vs 41 days outside it. For comparison, 2023: 780,000+ reports processed (+29% vs 2022), 88% never-seen-before, ~540,000 URLs classified illegal. ICCAM ('I See Child Abuse Material') was co-developed with INTERPOL. INHOPE is HOW a CSAM report made in one country reaches the hotline where content is hosted for fast removal, and it runs analyst training plus wellbeing/resilience programs (viewing CSAM is itself an occupational-trauma issue). Best citation for the global hotline architecture and for country-specific reporting routes so non-US/UK readers know where to report.

entities.name: Canadian Centre for Child Protection (C3P) — Project Arachnid & Cybertip.ca
entities.covers: Canadian charity operating Cybertip.ca (Canada's national tipline) and Project Arachnid, an automated crawler that detects known CSAM at scale and sends removal notices to hosts. Also runs survivor support and education (NeedHelpNow.ca, Commit to Kids, Kids in the Know).
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS (projectarachnid.ca / C3P, 2025 8-year milestone): since 2017 Project Arachnid has found, processed, and actioned nearly 50 million images/videos of CSAM and issued nearly 50 million removal notices to 1,500+ electronic service providers across 100+ countries (~13 million takedown notices in 2024-25 alone); it processes tens of thousands of images per second; it has identified 44,336 unique Tor onion services that directly hosted CSAM; C3P reported a backlog of 32.8 million+ suspect media awaiting assessment. Arachnid's data exposed how SLOW industry removal is and how often the same images recirculate. The analyst network spans 18 hotlines/organizations in 17 countries; the 'Shield by Project Arachnid' API gives ESPs proactive detection. SURVIVOR EVIDENCE (VERIFIED, C3P International Survivors' Survey, 400+ respondents as of Sept 2024): survivors whose abuse was recorded and distributed are re-victimized by every viewing; 30 respondents reported being IDENTIFIED in person by someone who had seen their abuse imagery; 56% said the abuse began before age four, 87% by age 11, and 58% had more than one abuser — the single best source for the 'permanent record / re-victimization-on-every-view' argument and for why takedown matters. C3P is also a leading critic of platform inaction and of end-to-end-encryption rollouts that block detection. Survivor/family resources: NeedHelpNow.ca, Cybertip.ca.

entities.name: Lucy Faithfull Foundation — Stop It Now! UK & Ireland
entities.covers: UK child-protection charity uniquely focused on PREVENTING child sexual abuse by working with people who have offended or fear they might, plus families and professionals. Runs the confidential Stop It Now helpline and anonymous self-help digital tools.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Fills the deterrence/help-seeking gap — the leading org explicitly oriented to people at risk of offending. VERIFIED FACTS: the Stop It Now UK helpline is 0808 1000 900 — confidential and anonymous (callers need not give a name, location, or contact details), staffed by trained professionals incl. psychologists and social workers; lines open Mon–Thu 9am–9pm, Fri 9am–5pm, with live chat and secure email (stopitnow.org.uk). VERIFIED USAGE (Lucy Faithfull Annual Report 2024/25): 8,435 people received advice/support via the helpline; service handled 19,161 calls, 19,349 emails, and 16,764 chats. It offers anonymous self-help modules for people looking at, or fearing they will look at, sexual images of children, paired with deterrence messaging that viewing CSAM is a serious crime that harms a real child; runs a regional Deterrence campaign (launched in Plymouth; 13,000+ people in Devon & Cornwall used Stop It Now resources in 2023). NOTE: the US 'Stop It Now!' is a separate allied org (helpline 1-888-773-8368). Best citation for prevention-of-offending and the 'there is confidential help if you're struggling with these urges' message.

entities.name: NSPCC (National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children)
entities.covers: Leading UK children's charity; runs Childline (counselling for children) and the adult NSPCC Helpline, plus major online-safety policy/advocacy (a primary campaigner behind the UK Online Safety Act 2023).
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS (NSPCC FOI data from all 45 UK police forces, pub. Oct 2024): 7,062 'Sexual Communication with a Child' offences were recorded in 2023/24 — up 89% since 2017/18, when the offence (won via NSPCC campaigning) was introduced; 41,021 online grooming crimes recorded UK-wide since 2017. Where the platform was known (1,824 cases), Snapchat was named in 48%, with Meta-owned platforms accounting for ~30% (WhatsApp 12%, Facebook/Messenger 12%, Instagram 6%); 81% of grooming cases targeted girls, and primary-school children (including a 4-year-old) were among victims. NSPCC also reported almost 87,000 child sexual offences recorded by UK police in 2022/23. CHILD-FACING: Childline is 0800 1111 (counselling for children, incl. sextortion and nudes); the adult NSPCC Helpline is 0808 800 5000. 'Report Remove' (NSPCC with IWF) lets a UK under-18 report a nude image of themselves for assessment and removal. Best UK citation for grooming-trend data with a platform breakdown.

entities.name: ECPAT International
entities.covers: Global network (~120+ member organizations in ~100+ countries) focused on ending the sexual exploitation of children in all forms — online CSEA, trafficking, exploitation in travel/tourism, child marriage. Co-leads the Disrupting Harm research program and stewards the authoritative terminology guidelines.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: TWO CITABLE ASSETS. (1) 'Disrupting Harm' — a research program by ECPAT + INTERPOL + UNICEF Office of Research–Innocenti (funded by Safe Online / End Violence); the core surveys covered nationally representative samples totaling 11,912 internet-using children aged 12–17 across 12 countries in Africa and Asia (2020–21), giving rare prevalence data on technology-facilitated CSEA in the Global South (with newer rounds expanding country coverage). (2) The 'Luxembourg Guidelines' (Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse) — initiated by ECPAT in 2014, deliberated over 18 months by an Interagency Working Group of 18 organizations, adopted 2016; the authoritative reference on WHY to say 'child sexual abuse material' not 'child pornography' (the latter implies a legitimacy/consent that cannot exist for a child) and on precise definitions of grooming, sextortion, live-streamed abuse, and self-generated content. The single best citation for correct, survivor-centered terminology — directly feeds the site's glossary.

entities.name: Stanford Internet Observatory (SIO) / Stanford Cyber Policy Center
entities.covers: Stanford University research program studying online abuse, with a major child-safety body of work. STATUS CAVEAT (verified): SIO was wound down in its prior form in 2024 amid lawsuits and political pressure — Alex Stamos departed and Renée DiResta's contract lapsed — but Stanford stated core child-safety/CSAM research (led by David Thiel) continues under the Cyber Policy Center; verify current hosting before citing. Key names: David Thiel, Alex Stamos, Renée DiResta, Riana Pfefferkorn, Shelby Grossman.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED CITABLE RESEARCH: (1) David Thiel's report 'Identifying and Eliminating CSAM in Generative ML Training Data and Models' (released Dec 20, 2023) found 1,008+ externally validated instances of CSAM (3,200+ suspected) in LAION-5B — the 5.85-billion-image dataset used to train Stable Diffusion 1.5 — detected via PhotoDNA/hash matching against NCMEC and C3P databases (researchers did not view images); LAION took the dataset offline in response, and later released a cleaned 'Re-LAION-5B.' This is the foundational evidence that generative-AI models can ingest real CSAM, and Thiel's team recommends NOT training general models on images of children at all. (2) 'Cross-Platform Dynamics of Self-Generated CSAM' (Thiel, DiResta, Stamos; June 6, 2023, with the Wall Street Journal and UMass Amherst) found large networks of accounts on Instagram (and to a lesser extent Twitter) openly advertising/selling self-generated CSAM, with Instagram's recommendation algorithms connecting and promoting them — the key citation for platform recommendation-system failure. (3) SIO's report on how to fix the CyberTipline pipeline (interviews with platforms, law enforcement, NGOs). (4) Pfefferkorn's work on encrypted-messaging safety / client-side-scanning tradeoffs and her 2025-26 caveat that NCMEC's 'Generative AI' report category is ambiguous and over-stated in the press. Best academic citation for AI-training-data and platform-recommendation problems.

entities.name: Childlight — Global Child Safety Institute (University of Edinburgh)
entities.covers: Research institute (launched 2023, University of Edinburgh, funded by the Human Dignity Foundation; partnered with UNSW Sydney) building the global evidence base on the scale and nature of child sexual abuse and exploitation. Publishes the 'Into the Light Index' and 'Searchlight.' Lead researcher: Prof. Debi Fry.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS (Into the Light Index, released May 27 2024; meta-analysis of 125 representative studies (2011–2023) plus 36M+ watchdog/policing reports; corroborated by University of Edinburgh, UNSW, the Guardian, GlobeNewswire): an estimated 302 million children — more than 300 million, 1 in 8 (12.6%) of children globally — were victims of non-consensual taking, sharing, or exposure to sexual images/video in the prior 12 months; a further 12.5% (~300 million) experienced online solicitation (unwanted sexual talk, requests for sexual acts or images) in the past year. PERPETRATION: 1 in 9 / 10.9% of US men (~14 million) admit having committed online sexual offenses against children at some point; 7% of UK men (~1.8 million) and 7.5% of Australian men (~700,000) say the same. The report frames CSA as a 'global health pandemic/emergency' and notes a file containing sexual images of a child is reported roughly every second. South Asia generates ~one-third of global CSAM hosting/upload alerts; standardized by population, North America and Western Europe rank among the highest CSAM-rate regions (with the US and Netherlands hosting high volumes). The NEWEST authoritative global-prevalence figure — highly quotable; cite precisely with the 2024 year and Childlight as source.

entities.name: INTERPOL — Crimes Against Children unit & ICSE Database
entities.covers: International police organization whose Crimes Against Children (CAC) unit runs victim identification and coordinates cross-border investigations. Maintains the International Child Sexual Exploitation (ICSE) image/video database connecting investigators across member countries.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS: as of March 2024, 38,825 children (victims) and 16,812 offenders were marked identified in the ICSE database (per INTERPOL CAC testimony to the US Congress); the database holds roughly 5–6 million images/videos and connects ~68–72 countries; by September 2025 INTERPOL reported 56,000+ victims and 24,000+ offenders identified — an average of 14 victims identified per day — with a target of 100,000 victims identified by 2030. ICSE uses image/video comparison software to link copies of the same abuse series across countries, avoiding duplicate investigation and saving time. INTERPOL runs Victim Identification Taskforces (specialist investigators working unsolved cases jointly) and maintains a 'Worst-of' baseline list of egregious domains/URLs for blocking. INHOPE's ICCAM connects to ICSE. Best citation for the law-enforcement / victim-rescue side and the global investigative database.

entities.name: Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force Program
entities.covers: US national network of coordinated regional task forces, funded by the DOJ Office of Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention (OJJDP), investigating and prosecuting technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation. Established 1998.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS (OJJDP, FY2024): 61 coordinated ICAC task forces represent more than 5,400 federal, state, and local law-enforcement and prosecutorial agencies across all 50 states; in FY2024 they conducted ~203,467 investigations leading to 12,600+ arrests, trained ~46,000 professionals, and were funded at $39.9 million. Task forces receive a large share of leads from NCMEC CyberTipline reports and conduct forensic exams, undercover/proactive operations, and prevention education; the annual 'Operation Broken Heart' alone has arrested 1,000+ offenders in a single push. Best US citation for 'who actually investigates a CyberTipline report locally' — directly relevant to for-first-responders and for-attorneys.

entities.name: National Center on Sexual Exploitation (NCOSE)
entities.covers: US advocacy nonprofit (formerly Morality in Media) opposing all forms of sexual exploitation incl. pornography, prostitution, trafficking, and image-based abuse. Runs the annual 'Dirty Dozen List' and the NCOSE Law Center, which litigates against platforms.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Treat as ADVOCACY (medium authority — clearly a point of view; some NCOSE claims about pornography are contested in the clinical literature). VERIFIED FACTUAL MILESTONE: following Nicholas Kristof's Dec 2020 NYT column 'The Children of Pornhub,' Visa and Mastercard suspended payment processing on Pornhub and MindGeek removed all content from unverified uploaders — the catalog fell from ~13.5 million videos to ~2.9–4.7 million over a weekend (roughly 80% removed) — then required uploader verification and banned downloads; NCOSE campaigning (it brought CSAM/trafficking evidence to Visa in early 2020) helped drive this. The Dirty Dozen List (annual since 2013) has targeted Pornhub/MindGeek, Twitter/X, Meta, Snapchat, TikTok, Discord, Roblox, Amazon, Google/GitHub, LinkedIn, and others; the 2025 list pivoted to a campaign to repeal Section 230. NCOSE Law Center files civil suits for trafficking/CSAM survivors under 18 U.S.C. 2255/TVPRA. Use NCOSE for the verified Pornhub-purge policy fact and as the 'abolitionist-advocacy perspective,' not for clinical claims.

entities.name: Detection infrastructure — PhotoDNA (Microsoft / Hany Farid) and open hashing standards
entities.covers: The core detection technologies the whole ecosystem depends on. Not an org but a critical knowledge node: PhotoDNA (Microsoft Research + Dartmouth's Hany Farid, ~2009), plus Google's CSAI Match (video) and Content Safety API, Apple's NeuralHash (withdrawn 2021-22), and Meta's open-sourced PDQ (photo) and TMK+PDQF (video) hashes (2019).
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED FOUNDATIONAL TECHNICAL KNOWLEDGE for a 'how detection works' explainer: (1) PhotoDNA converts an image to greyscale, divides it into a grid, and computes intensity gradients to produce a robust ~1152-bit PERCEPTUAL hash that survives resizing/cropping/recoloring — so known CSAM is matched even when altered, without humans re-viewing it; matching is against vetted hash sets (NCMEC maintains the US database). Microsoft provides PhotoDNA free to qualifying organizations; it is used by Google/Gmail, Facebook, Twitter/X, Reddit, Discord, Adobe, and others. (2) The crucial public distinction: hash-matching finds KNOWN material; AI classifiers (Google Content Safety API / CSAI Match, Thorn Safer Predict, IWF classifier) find NOVEL material but produce false positives needing human review. (3) Hany Farid (UC Berkeley) is the key named expert on perceptual hashing. (4) Meta open-sourced PDQ/TMK+PDQF in 2019 so smaller platforms can match content. (5) Caveat to note: researchers have demonstrated collision attacks against PhotoDNA and NeuralHash, and client-side scanning remains contested on privacy grounds. Anchors a strong net-new 'detection infrastructure' page and supports for-developers and ai-csam-response.

entities.name: Safe Online (Global Partnership to End Violence Against Children)
entities.covers: The world's largest dedicated funder of initiatives to keep children safe online (housed within the End Violence Partnership). Funds research, technology, and frontline programs against online CSEA, with a strong focus on low- and middle-income countries.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS (safeonline.global): since 2016 Safe Online has invested over US$100 million across ~106 projects with impact in 100 countries; in 2024 it awarded ~$10M to 23 new grantees (from a 2023 Open Call) and invested ~$16M across 50+ projects, expanding into Gen-AI and child-safety research. It funded the Disrupting Harm research program and many CSAM-detection/hotline-capacity projects in the Global South, and co-runs the Safe Online Research Fund with the Tech Coalition (which added a further $1M). Best citation for the funding ecosystem and Global-South capacity-building — useful for international-resources.

entities.name: Marie Collins Foundation
entities.covers: UK charity (founded 2011, named after survivor-advocate Marie Collins) focused specifically on supporting children/young people who have experienced technology-assisted child sexual abuse (TA-CSA) — online grooming, livestreamed abuse, and the trauma of having abuse imagery shared — and on training professionals to respond.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Fills a victim-support specialism the larger orgs don't: it centers the distinct, ongoing trauma of survivors whose abuse was recorded and circulated ('it never ends because the images are still out there'), defines and explains Technology-Assisted Child Sexual Abuse (TA-CSA), and delivers specialist victim-focused, recovery-oriented training to UK and international professionals (social workers, healthcare, educators, law enforcement). Best citation for trauma-informed support of tech-facilitated-abuse survivors specifically — complements for-victims and for-clinicians.

entities.name: Stop It Now! (USA)
entities.covers: US (Massachusetts-based) child-sexual-abuse-prevention nonprofit running a confidential helpline for adults concerned about their own or another's behavior toward children, plus prevention guides.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED RESOURCE: the Stop It Now USA helpline is 1-888-PREVENT (1-888-773-8368), with email and live-chat, providing confidential support for people worried about their own sexual thoughts/behaviors toward children, concerned family members, and survivors' families; publishes 'Warning Signs' guides (concerning adult and child behaviors) and safety-planning resources. The best US-specific deterrence/help-seeking hotline to list alongside Lucy Faithfull (UK) on for-offenders and prevention pages.

entities.name: RAINN (Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network)
entities.covers: Largest US anti-sexual-violence organization; operates the National Sexual Assault Hotline and the DoD Safe Helpline, with survivor support and prevention education.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED RESOURCE: National Sexual Assault Hotline 1-800-656-HOPE (1-800-656-4673) and online.rainn.org chat — free, confidential, 24/7, routing callers to local providers. RAINN publishes frequently cited US child-sexual-abuse statistics (confirm current figures/methodology at rainn.org/statistics). A useful survivor-support citation that complements for-victims, though general sexual-violence rather than CSAM-specific.

recommended_additions: CSAM Prevention Organizations Directory (net-new) — a single authoritative 'who's who' page mapping the ecosystem by FUNCTION (reporting hotlines, detection-tech providers, investigative/law-enforcement, research institutes, deterrence/help-seeking, policy/standards, survivor support), with each org's mandate, region, and how to reach/report to it. No existing page is a directory of the institutions themselves; highest-leverage gap.

How CSAM Detection Actually Works (net-new technical explainer) — perceptual hashing (PhotoDNA, Meta PDQ/TMK+PDQF, the withdrawn Apple NeuralHash), classifiers for novel content (Google CSAI/Content Safety API, Thorn Safer Predict, IWF classifier), hash-/signal-sharing (NCMEC, IWF, Tech Coalition Lantern, INHOPE ICCAM, INTERPOL ICSE), and the KNOWN-vs-NOVEL distinction with false-positive/human-review and collision-attack/E2EE tradeoffs. Complements for-developers and ai-csam-response.

Confidential Help If You're Struggling (net-new, deterrence/help-seeking) — a non-judgmental page pointing people worried about their own thoughts/behavior toward children to Lucy Faithfull / Stop It Now UK (0808 1000 900; 8,435 helped in 2024/25) and Stop It Now USA (1-888-773-8368), pairing deterrence ('viewing CSAM is a serious crime that harms a real child every time') with a concrete route to help. Sharpens for-offenders and prevention-programs.

Global Policy & Standards Landscape (net-new) — WeProtect Model National Response and Global Threat Assessment (87% rise since 2019), the EU CSA Regulation / 'Chat Control' debate, UK Online Safety Act 2023, the US REPORT Act (2024), the client-side-scanning vs. end-to-end-encryption tradeoff, and the Thorn/All Tech Is Human Safety-by-Design-for-GenAI principles + 2025 progress report. Complements for-compliance-teams and for-tech-ceos.

The Permanent Record: Survivor Harm from Circulated Imagery (net-new, or a section within for-victims) — built on C3P's International Survivors' Survey (30 survivors identified in person by someone who saw their imagery; abuse began before age 4 for 56%) and the Marie Collins Foundation, documenting re-victimization-on-every-view and grounding the case for takedown tools (NCMEC Take It Down, NSPCC/IWF Report Remove, StopNCII). Complements for-victims and report-csam.

Where to Report by Country (expansion of international-resources) — concrete routes via INHOPE's 55-hotline / 51-country network (1.4-day in-network vs 41-day out-of-network removal), Cybertip.ca (Canada), IWF (UK), plus INTERPOL/ICSE context, so non-US/UK readers know exactly where to go. Complements international-resources and report-csam.

Correct Terminology & Why It Matters (expansion of glossary) — adopt ECPAT's Luxembourg Guidelines: 'child sexual abuse material' not 'child pornography,' with precise definitions of grooming, sextortion, self-generated content, capping, and live-streamed abuse. Complements glossary.

The Generative-AI CSAM Threat, with an accuracy caveat (expansion of ai-csam-response) — fold in IWF's 2024 AI data (245 reports / 7,644 images actioned, first realistic AI videos, fine-tuned Stable Diffusion generating known victims on demand), Stanford's LAION-5B finding (1,008+ validated instances; dataset pulled, Re-LAION released), NCMEC's 1,325% GAI report surge AND Pfefferkorn's caveat that the 'Generative AI' report category is ambiguous and over-stated in the press. Complements ai-csam-response.

The Numbers, In Context (net-new, or a maintained section of news/research-feed) — a dated statistics page: NCMEC 20.5M reports (2024) / 21.3M (2025); IWF 291,270 webpages (2024); Childlight ~302M children/year (2024); Project Arachnid ~50M removal notices since 2017 (~13M in 2024-25); INTERPOL 38,825 victims identified (Mar 2024) rising to 56,000+ (Sept 2025); INHOPE 2.5M ICCAM records (2024); NSPCC 7,062 grooming offences (2023/24, +89%); ICAC 12,600+ arrests (FY2024) — each with source and year, with the NCMEC 'bundling' and GAI-category caveats explained so the site is the place that gets the numbers RIGHT. Complements news and research-feed.
findings.highest_value_gap: The site has issue-specific pages (report-csam, ai-csam-response, prevention-programs) but no authoritative directory of the ORGANIZATIONS and detection/reporting INFRASTRUCTURE that make up the child-safety ecosystem — i.e., a single page that tells a reader who NCMEC, IWF, Thorn, INHOPE, the Tech Coalition (Lantern), the Canadian Centre (Project Arachnid), Lucy Faithfull / Stop It Now, WeProtect, ECPAT, INTERPOL, and ICAC actually are, what each does, and how to reach or report to each, plus an honest 'how detection works' explainer (hash-matching for KNOWN content vs. classifiers for NOVEL content). That who's-who-and-how-it-works map is the single most important missing piece: it turns the existing topical pages into a navigable, citable, trustworthy resource, and it is exactly what competitor sites in this space conspicuously lack. A strong secondary differentiator is a maintained, properly-caveated statistics page — the verified 2024-2025 numbers here (NCMEC 20.5M reports in 2024 / 21.3M in 2025 and the 1,325% GAI surge; IWF 291,270 webpages and 245 AI-CSAM reports; Childlight ~302M children/year; Project Arachnid ~50M removal notices since 2017; INTERPOL 38,825 victims identified by March 2024; INHOPE 2.5M ICCAM records with 1.4-day vs 41-day removal times; NSPCC 7,062 grooming offences, +89%; ICAC 12,600+ FY2024 arrests) come with two crucial nuances most outlets get wrong — the NCMEC 'bundling' artifact behind the apparent 2024 drop, and Stanford/Pfefferkorn's warning that the 'Generative AI' CyberTipline category is ambiguous and overstated in headlines — so being the site that reports them correctly is a real authority advantage. All statistics in this submission were verified against primary or first-tier sources (NCMEC, IWF, Thorn/Safer, INHOPE, C3P/Project Arachnid, INTERPOL, OJJDP, Childlight/University of Edinburgh, NSPCC, WeProtect, Safe Online) during research; each should still be re-checked against its source's latest figures before publication, since several orgs update annually.

entities.name: Prevention Project Dunkelfeld / Kein Täter werden (Institute of Sexology and Sexual Medicine, Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin)
entities.covers: The pioneering demand-side primary/secondary prevention program (launched June 2005, Berlin) offering free, confidential CBT-based treatment to people sexually attracted to children who are not known to the justice system. Led by sexologist Prof. Klaus M. Beier; now a national network of 13 treatment sites across Germany.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS: Launched June 2005 at Charité Berlin, lead researcher Prof. Klaus M. Beier. 'Dunkelfeld' = 'dark field,' the hidden population of undetected/at-risk individuals. By 2010, 1,134 people had responded to the media campaign; 499 completed full diagnostic assessment; 255 were offered a therapy place (Beier et al.). In the first three years, 808 people contacted the project. Between 2005-2011, 319 undetected help-seekers entered the ~1-year CBT treatment program. The network reports ~20,000 anonymous contacts over its first 20 years. Now 13 treatment facilities nationwide. Treatment = manualized Berlin Dissexuality Therapy (BEDIT): ~1 year CBT group therapy targeting coping skills, emotion regulation, victim empathy, and offense-supportive cognitions, with optional pharmacotherapy (SSRIs, anti-androgens). FUNDING: initially Volkswagen Foundation, then German federal support from 2008; guaranteed financing via German Social Code (health insurance funds) through 2025 at ~€5 million/year. LEGAL: Germany has no mandatory reporting of undisclosed/undetected offenses revealed in therapy (medical confidentiality / Schweigepflicht) — the program argues this is what makes confidential help-seeking possible, in sharp contrast with the US. Campaign tagline: 'You are not guilty because of your desire, but you are responsible for your behavior. Don't become an offender.' EVIDENCE IS CONTESTED — must present alongside the Mokros & Banse (2019) reanalysis (no demonstrated treatment-specific effect) and the 2024 follow-up registry findings (see below).

entities.name: Dunkelfeld follow-up & iatrogenic-effect debate (Journal of Prevention, 2024-2025)
entities.covers: The current (2024-2025) evidence picture for the Dunkelfeld approach: long-term registry-based recidivism data plus a published concern about possible iatrogenic effects and a public-health rebuttal — the citable basis for describing the program honestly rather than promotionally.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED: 2024 follow-up (Springer Journal of Prevention, open access via PMC11568044, 'Preventing Child Sexual Abuse and the Use of Child Sexual Abuse Materials: Following up on the German Prevention Project Dunkelfeld') reports, using German registry data, minimal OFFICIAL recidivism: 1.1% for contact CSA and 5.7% for CSAM after 6 years. BUT across PPD studies, treatment produced only small-to-moderate changes in dynamic risk factors and SELF-REPORTED relapse during treatment/follow-up was high: 14-20% for contact CSA and 39-90.6% for CSAM (12-28 month follow-ups) — prompting published concern about potential iatrogenic effects of the Dunkelfeld model. König (2025, 'The German Dunkelfeld Approach: When the Dark Figure... Remains Shady', Journal of Prevention, PMC12289709) is the critical paper; Beier's team published a public-health rebuttal ('A Public Health Imperative Requiring Context-Appropriate Science — A Response to König (2025)', doi 10.1007/s10935-025-00859-6). Holper et al. (2024) meta-analysis warns that risk-focused treatment of LOW-risk sexual offenders can significantly INCREASE sexual recidivism — a crucial nuance for any treatment page. This cluster is the honest 'does it actually work?' counterweight.

entities.name: Mokros & Banse (2019) — 'The Dunkelfeld Project for Self-Identified Pedophiles: A Reappraisal of its Effectiveness' (Journal of Sexual Medicine)
entities.covers: The most important single critical reanalysis of the Dunkelfeld treatment data — found no evidence the treatment reduces proneness to offend — essential for credibility.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED: Andreas Mokros & Rainer Banse, J Sex Med, 2019;16(5):609. Reanalyzed Beier et al.'s PPD outcome data and concluded 'the data do not show that treatment within the Dunkelfeld program leads to any reduction of the proneness to commit sexual offenses against children' on dynamic risk factors. They note the reappraisal shares the original's limited statistical power, so effectiveness cannot be definitively ruled out either — but the positive claims are unsupported. Honest takeaway for the site: help-seeking is protective and the model is ethically compelling, but RCT-grade proof that treatment reduces actual offending does not yet exist (and a no-treatment control arm is ethically fraught). Presenting this is what separates an authoritative resource from advocacy.

entities.name: Troubled Desire (troubled-desire.com) — Charité Berlin
entities.covers: Free, anonymous, multilingual web-based self-assessment and self-management tool for people with pedophilic/hebephilic sexual interest, built by the Charité/Dunkelfeld team to extend the approach globally to jurisdictions with no in-person services.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS: Developed under Prof. Klaus M. Beier, based on 10+ years of Dunkelfeld treatment experience; launched Oct 2017; available in 7 languages. In its first 30 months (25 Oct 2017 – 25 Apr 2020) the self-assessment was completed by 4,161 users worldwide; accesses came mainly from Germany (54.7%) and the USA (11.4%). Of users, 78.9% (n=3,281) reported pedophilic/hebephilic interest; of those, 72.8% (n=2,390) had used CSAM and 41.5% (n=1,363) reported having sexually abused a child. This is the most directly linkable GLOBAL self-help tool and is already name-dropped (one line) on our /for-offenders stub — it deserves a real, statistic-backed description. Source: Internet-based Self-management Tool study (Beier et al.).

entities.name: Lucy Faithfull Foundation
entities.covers: The only UK-wide child-protection charity focused solely on preventing child sexual abuse. Operates the Stop It Now UK & Ireland helpline and self-help resources, runs the UK online deterrence campaign, and partners on the reThink chatbot. Founded ~1992 (30+ years).
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS (2024/25 Annual Report): 8,435 people received advice/support through the Stop It Now helpline; the Foundation supported 16,000+ people across the UK via direct work, online, and the helpline; it worked with 373 men arrested for online sexual offences and 325 affected family members (plus 1,019 active Family & Friends Forum users); 1.8 million+ website visits. In 2025, 330,000+ people sought support over their own or someone else's online sexual behavior toward children — a 20% rise on 2024. In 2023, ~217,889 people contacted the helpline or Get Help self-help resources. The Foundation publishes a yearly Annual Review (cite the specific year). 2024/25 report PDF: https://www.lucyfaithfull.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Annual-Report-2024-25.pdf

entities.name: Stop It Now! UK & Ireland (Lucy Faithfull Foundation)
entities.covers: Confidential, anonymous helpline and self-help resources for people worried about their own sexual thoughts/behavior toward children or compulsive viewing of illegal images — the operational front door of the UK demand-side model, plus the UK online deterrence campaign.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED: UK/Ireland helpline 0808 1000 900 (freephone) plus secure messaging; fully anonymous, callers need not identify themselves. The Stop It Now! deterrence campaign launched October 2015 (online warning messages/ads steering people away from CSAM toward help). 2023/24 Annual Report: 536 people contacted the helpline saying they had not harmed a child but were worried about their sexual thoughts toward children and risk of a contact offence; 279 called about someone else they were worried about; the Shore website for teenagers had 25,000+ users and 106 direct contacts. Already on our /for-offenders stub but only as a bare phone number — the page should explain what actually happens on a call (anonymous, non-judgmental, focused on keeping everyone safe), since shame/fear is the biggest barrier to help-seeking.

entities.name: Newman et al. (2024) — evaluation of the UK Stop It Now! deterrence campaign (Sexual Abuse)
entities.covers: The peer-reviewed effectiveness evaluation of the UK's online deterrence campaign — citable evidence that public-health deterrence drives help-seeking and self-reported behavior change.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED: Newman, Efthymiadou, Quayle, Squire, Denis, Wortley, Beier, Koukopoulos (2024), 'The Impact of a Public Health Campaign to Deter Viewing of Child Sexual Abuse Images Online: A Case Study of the UK Stop It Now! Campaign,' Sexual Abuse (open access PMC11311905). Drew on 11,190 unique helpline callers and 109,432 new website visitors (2015-2018) plus 3 website surveys (N=252). Among pre-arrest survey respondents, 77.8% reported they had stopped viewing online sexual abuse images of children and 55.6% had engaged with the Foundation. CAVEAT to fold in: small survey N and anonymous self-report limit causal claims — present as encouraging but not definitive. Note the author list bridges Edinburgh, Lucy Faithfull, and Charité/Beier.

entities.name: Protect Children (Suojellaan Lapsia ry) — ReDirection project & self-help program
entities.covers: Finnish NGO running the ReDirection project: the 'Help Us to Help You' anonymous dark-web survey of CSAM users (one of the largest datasets of its kind) and a free, anonymous, CBT-based self-help program delivered directly on the dark web in multiple languages.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS: ReDirection launched 2020; surveys placed directly on the dark web ('Help us to help you' and 'No need for help'). 26,000+ total survey responses since 2020. Headline findings: 50% would like to stop viewing/searching/sharing CSAM (a 2024 peer-reviewed sample of 4,493 found 55.0%); 62% have already tried to stop but failed; 52% feared their CSAM use would lead to an in-person (contact) offence; 37% have sought direct contact with a child online and 44% have at least once thought about it; 70% were under 18 when they first saw CSAM and ~40% were under 13. Help-seeking gap is the core message: only ~13.8-28% have sought or considered help and only ~3% (3.2% in 2024) actually received it. THE SELF-HELP PROGRAM: free, anonymous, CBT-based, 5 modules (Pathways to CSAM; My Life and My Use; My Risk Management; ReDirection of My Life; Next Steps); 7 languages (English, Spanish, Polish, Finnish, Latvian, Croatian, Italian); opened 70,000+ times; 74% of program users reported ceasing or reducing CSAM consumption. Lead researchers Tia (Tegan) Insoll & Anna K. Soriano Ovaska; Exec. Director Nina Vaaranen-Valkonen; dark-web research with Juha Nurmi (Ahmia/Tampere Univ.). Funders/partners include Safe Online / End Violence Against Children and the Tech Coalition. Program site: https://www.redirectionprogram.com/

entities.name: Insoll et al. — dark-web CSAM-user studies (Journal of Online Trust and Safety, 2022 & 2024)
entities.covers: The peer-reviewed academic backbone for Protect Children's statistics — the citable, primary sources for what CSAM users themselves report about escalation risk, contact-seeking, and desire to stop.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED: (1) Insoll, Ovaska, Nurmi, Aaltonen & Vaaranen-Valkonen (2022), 'Risk Factors for Child Sexual Abuse Material Users Contacting Children Online: Results of an Anonymous Multilingual Survey on the Dark Web,' Journal of Online Trust and Safety 1(2), doi 10.54501/jots.v1i2.29 — base analytic sample n=1,546; sources for the 52% fear-of-contact, 37% sought-contact, 44% considered-contact figures. (2) Insoll et al. (2024), 'Factors Associated with Help-Seeking Among Online CSAM Offenders,' Journal of Online Trust and Safety — n=4,493; 55.0% want to stop, 13.8% sought help, 3.2% accessed help. Both are directly citable; quote N and percentages to the paper's precision. (Note: an earlier broad citation to a 'Frontiers in Psychology 2022' paper appears to be a mis-attribution — the canonical peer-reviewed venue is the Journal of Online Trust and Safety; cite that.)

entities.name: reThink Chatbot (Internet Watch Foundation + Lucy Faithfull Foundation + Aylo/Pornhub)
entities.covers: A point-of-search deterrence intervention: when a user searches CSAM-associated terms on Pornhub UK, a chatbot/warning interrupts and redirects toward Stop It Now — a real-world, independently evaluated demand-side deterrence experiment with published numbers.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED HARD STATS (independent evaluation led by University of Tasmania, Feb 2024): collaboration of IWF, Lucy Faithfull Foundation, and Aylo (formerly MindGeek). ~5 million warning messages displayed on Pornhub UK from July 2021 onward; chatbot sessions ~2.19M-2.79M depending on data source (IWF reported 2,768,206 sessions; Aylo Google Analytics 2,192,096; a May 2022-Apr 2023 export logged 2,787,094 displays). 1,656 requests for more information were made via the chatbot and 490 people clicked through to the Stop It Now website; hundreds contacted the helpline. The evaluation found the warning/chatbot REDUCED total CSAM searches on Pornhub, and most sessions that triggered the warning did not search for such images again. Evaluation report PDF: https://www.lucyfaithfull.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/reThink_Chatbot_Evaluation_Report.pdf . This is the strongest concrete evidence for platform-side deterrence — fold into /ai-csam-response and /for-tech-ceos.

entities.name: Moore Center for the Prevention of Child Sexual Abuse, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health — 'Help Wanted' Prevention Intervention
entities.covers: Leading US academic primary-prevention intervention: an anonymous, online, self-paced course for adolescents and young adults attracted to children, built on the public-health premise that attraction is distinct from offending and early support prevents first-time offending.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED: Directed by Prof. Elizabeth Letourneau. 'Help Wanted' is a free, anonymous online course developed from qualitative interviews with young adults attracted to prepubescent children who had NO support during adolescence; supported by the Moore Center and RALIANCE. A randomized evaluation is underway (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06300957, 'Help Wanted: Evaluating a Prevention Intervention for People With Sexual Interest in Children'). In 2021 the Moore Center received a $10.3M grant for global prevention work. Letourneau's framing: 'having the attraction does not doom a person to acting on that attraction,' and stigma itself impedes prevention. This is the flagship US academic equivalent of Dunkelfeld and is COMPLETELY ABSENT from our site, which currently skews UK/Germany — a major geographic and substantive gap. Org page: https://publichealth.jhu.edu/moore-center-for-the-prevention-of-child-sexual-abuse

entities.name: StopSO (Specialist Treatment Organisation for the Prevention of Sexual Offending)
entities.covers: UK charity that connects people worried about their sexual thoughts/behavior — before or after offending, including online behavior — with a national network of trained, vetted therapists for confidential self-referred therapy, filling the near-total NHS gap for this population.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED: Self-referral model; matches clients to therapists trained to work with this group (members complete 16 hours CPD/year, 5 of them face-to-face specific to this client group). Note StopSO's own framing that 'there are practically no NHS services' for people who have or might commit sexual offences. Founded by Juliet Grayson. Sits between an anonymous helpline and intensive statutory treatment. Not mentioned on our site. Pair with a note on the risk-assessment tools standard in this field (Static-99R, STABLE-2007) and the cautionary UK Ministry of Justice finding (Mews, Di Bella & Purver, 2017) that the prison Core Sex Offender Treatment Programme was associated with slightly HIGHER reoffending — reinforcing that 'treatment' is not uniformly effective.

entities.name: Stop It Now USA (Safer Society Foundation)
entities.covers: US confidential helpline and resources for adults concerned about their own or another adult's behavior toward children — the closest US analogue to the UK helpline, operating under a different (mandatory-reporting) legal regime.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED: US helpline 1-888-773-8368 (already on our /for-offenders stub). CRITICAL distinction to explain honestly: US clinicians face mandatory child-abuse reporting duties, so the confidentiality promise differs sharply from Germany (no reporting of undisclosed offenses) and the UK (anonymous helpline). A public resource should state plainly what is and isn't confidential in the US so people aren't misled into a false sense of safety. This three-way legal contrast (Germany / UK / US) is itself a high-value explainer that no existing page covers.

recommended_additions: Expand /prevention-programs from stub into the flagship 'demand-side / primary prevention' hub — it already introduces the primary/secondary/tertiary framework and Dunkelfeld but ends as a stub; build it out with Dunkelfeld+BEDIT (1,134 campaign responses by 2010; ~20,000 contacts in 20 years; 13 sites; €5M/yr), Troubled Desire (4,161 users in first 30 months), ReDirection (26,000+ survey responses; program opened 70,000+ times; 74% reduced/ceased), Help Wanted, StopSO, and the reThink chatbot — each with year-stamped stats and citations. (Expands existing page.)

Add an 'Does prevention treatment actually work? Evidence and honest limitations' section/sub-page — net-new angle no current page carries; present the Mokros & Banse (2019) reappraisal (no demonstrated treatment effect), the 2024 registry follow-up (1.1% official CSA recidivism / 5.7% CSAM but high self-reported relapse and an iatrogenic-effects debate, König 2025 vs Beier rebuttal), Holper et al. (2024) on risk-focused treatment harming low-risk individuals, and the 2017 MoJ SOTP finding. This intellectual honesty is what makes the resource authoritative rather than promotional. (Net-new; complements /prevention-programs, /the-science, /treatment-modalities.)

Rebuild /for-offenders into a real, action-oriented 'get help before you harm' page — currently a stub with bare contact details; explain concretely what happens when you contact Stop It Now UK (0808 1000 900, anonymous), Stop It Now USA (1-888-773-8368), Troubled Desire, ReDirection, or Help Wanted — anonymity, non-judgment, and exactly what is/isn't confidential — because shame and fear of exposure are the dominant barriers (only ~3% of dark-web CSAM users who want help actually get it). (Expands existing page.)

Add a 'Confidentiality and the law: can you get help anonymously?' explainer covering Germany (no mandatory reporting of undisclosed offenses) vs UK (anonymous helpline) vs US (clinician mandatory reporting) — this legal difference is decisive for whether at-risk people reach out, is referenced nowhere coherently, and bridges /for-offenders, /for-clinicians, and /for-attorneys. (Net-new; cross-links three existing pages.)

Add a dedicated 'Help for people attracted to minors' primary-prevention page that carefully distinguishes attraction from offending — the Moore Center 'Help Wanted' model and the Dunkelfeld premise both rest on this distinction; cover stigma/isolation/suicidality data, Letourneau's 'attraction does not doom a person to offend' framing, and the prevention rationale. Serves a population the site barely addresses and anchors the US dimension currently missing. (Net-new; complements /for-offenders and /prevention-programs.)

Fold the reThink chatbot and Protect Children dark-web findings into /ai-csam-response and /for-tech-ceos — those pages cover platform/tech response but lack a concrete, independently evaluated point-of-search deterrence model (~5M warnings on Pornhub UK; reduced CSAM searches; 490 click-throughs to Stop It Now) and the data showing CSAM users themselves want to stop (50-55%) and fear escalation (52%). Directly relevant supporting evidence. (Expands existing pages.)
findings.highest_value_gap: Our site treats demand-side prevention as two thin stubs (/prevention-programs and /for-offenders) that name-drop Dunkelfeld and Stop It Now without the substance that makes them credible or actionable: no hard statistics, no description of how the programs actually work, no US program at all (the Johns Hopkins Moore Center 'Help Wanted' and Stop It Now USA are entirely absent), and — most damaging for authority — no honest engagement with the contested evidence base. The single highest-value move is to build one rigorous, fully-cited 'demand-side / primary prevention' hub plus an 'honest limitations' companion that (a) describes each program concretely with year-stamped statistics (Dunkelfeld: 1,134 campaign responses by 2010, ~20,000 contacts in 20 years, 13 sites, €5M/yr; Troubled Desire: 4,161 users in 30 months; ReDirection: 26,000+ survey responses, program opened 70,000+ times, 74% reduced/ceased use; reThink: ~5M warnings, reduced searches; Stop It Now UK: 8,435 helpline contacts in 2024/25), (b) explains the Germany/UK/US confidentiality-and-law differences that determine whether at-risk people dare to reach out, and (c) presents the limitations honestly (Mokros & Banse 2019 found no demonstrated treatment effect; the 2024 registry follow-up shows low official recidivism but a live iatrogenic-effects debate; no RCT-grade proof that treatment reduces offending yet exists, with one underway via Help Wanted). That combination — actionable, statistic-backed help routes plus intellectual honesty about the evidence — is exactly what no competitor page does well and what a public-health resource must do to be trusted.

entities.name: Joshua B. Grubbs, PhD
entities.covers: Psychologist (University of New Mexico, formerly Bowling Green State). Leading researcher on 'moral incongruence' and self-perceived pornography addiction. Co-developed the Cyber-Pornography Use Inventory and studies on perceived addiction vs. actual dysregulation.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Grubbs, Perry, Wilt & Reid (2019), 'Pornography Problems Due to Moral Incongruence: An Integrative Model with a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis,' Archives of Sexual Behavior 48(2):397-415 — the meta-analysis found religiosity and moral disapproval are robustly (often more strongly than frequency of use) associated with SELF-PERCEIVED porn addiction. Two-pathway model: distress from (1) genuine dysregulation AND (2) moral incongruence (PPMI). Also Grubbs & Gola (2019, J Sexual Medicine) found NO robust longitudinal link between porn use and erectile functioning. This is the single most important framework an honest resource must represent: many who self-label 'addicted' are experiencing shame/values conflict, not a substance-like addiction.

entities.name: Nicole Prause, PhD
entities.covers: Neuroscientist, founder of Liberos LLC. Most prominent scientific skeptic of the 'porn addiction'/cue-reactivity model; studies sexual arousal using EEG/physiology.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Steele, Staley, Sabatinelli & Prause (2013), 'Sexual desire, not hypersexuality...' Socioaffective Neuroscience & Psychology — EEG P300 to sexual images in self-identified hypersexuals correlated with sexual DESIRE, not hypersexuality severity (opposite of addiction prediction). Prause, Steele, Staley, Sabatinelli & Hajcak (2015), 'Modulation of late positive potentials by sexual images in problem users and controls inconsistent with porn addiction,' Biological Psychology — problem users showed LOWER LPP to sexual cues than controls (opposite of drug cue-reactivity). Co-author with Ley & Finn of 'The Emperor Has No Clothes.' Note: was in a public/legal trademark dispute with Gary Wilson and runs a critique counter-site (RealYBOP).

entities.name: David J. Ley, PhD
entities.covers: Clinical psychologist, leading critic of the sex/porn addiction model. Author and Psychology Today contributor.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Book: 'The Myth of Sex Addiction' (2012, Rowman & Littlefield) — argues sex addiction is a social construct that pathologizes high sexual desire and can excuse infidelity. Ley, Prause & Finn (2014), 'The Emperor Has No Clothes: A Review of the Pornography Addiction Model,' Current Sexual Health Reports 6:94-105 — central skeptic review: studies are mostly correlational/cross-sectional, lack controls, 'withdrawal'/'tolerance' poorly demonstrated, self-reported addiction tracks religiosity more than use. Argues the addiction label itself can harm by amplifying shame.

entities.name: Shane W. Kraus, PhD
entities.covers: Director, Behavioral Addictions Lab, University of Nevada Las Vegas. Lead author of the ICD-11 CSBD description; centrist 'evidence-first' voice who helped craft the diagnosis.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Kraus, Krueger, Briken, First...Reed (2018), 'Compulsive sexual behaviour disorder in the ICD-11,' World Psychiatry 17(1):109-110 — the foundational description. Kraus, Voon & Potenza (2016), 'Should compulsive sexual behavior be considered an addiction?' Addiction 111(12):2097-2106 — concluded CSB shares addiction features but evidence gaps preclude definitive 'addiction' classification. His group helped develop/validate the CSBD-19 scale. Represents the official middle position: the condition is real and impairing (warrants a diagnosis) but the addiction label is premature.

entities.name: Valerie Voon, MD, PhD
entities.covers: Neuropsychiatrist, University of Cambridge. Ran the landmark fMRI study of brain cue-reactivity in compulsive sexual behaviour.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Voon et al. (2014), 'Neural Correlates of Sexual Cue Reactivity in Individuals with and without Compulsive Sexual Behaviours,' PLoS ONE 9(7):e102419 — men with CSB showed sexual-cue reactivity in ventral striatum, dorsal anterior cingulate and amygdala (the same network as drug-cue reactivity); activity tracked subjective wanting/desire more than liking (incentive-salience model). Cited by BOTH sides. Important nuance: Voon cautioned it does NOT prove porn is 'addictive' — only that brain patterns resemble addiction. Featured in Channel 4's 'Porn on the Brain.'

entities.name: Matthias Brand, PhD
entities.covers: University of Duisburg-Essen (Germany). Cognitive neuroscientist; created the I-PACE model, the dominant theoretical framework for problematic internet/porn use.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Brand, Young, Laier, Wolfling & Potenza (2016), 'Integrating psychological and neurobiological considerations...I-PACE model,' Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews 71:252-266 (updated 2019). I-PACE = Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution: predisposing variables x cue-reactivity/craving/attentional bias x reduced inhibitory control, with conditioning/habit formation over time. Represents the scientific position that problematic porn use fits a behavioral-addiction framework. Essential for representing the pro-addiction-model camp rigorously.

entities.name: Rory C. Reid, PhD
entities.covers: UCLA (Semel Institute). Led the DSM-5 field trial for Hypersexual Disorder.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Reid et al. (2012), 'Report of findings in a DSM-5 field trial for hypersexual disorder,' J Sexual Medicine 9(11):2868-2877 — proposed criteria showed good reliability/validity. CRITICAL FACT: despite this, the American Psychiatric Association REJECTED Hypersexual Disorder from DSM-5 (2013), citing insufficient evidence, forensic-misuse concerns, and risk of pathologizing normal behavior. Original proposal: Kafka (2010), Archives of Sexual Behavior.

entities.name: Paul J. Wright, PhD
entities.covers: Indiana University communication scientist; leading meta-analyst of pornography's effects on attitudes, satisfaction, and aggression.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Wright, Tokunaga & Kraus (2016), meta-analysis in J Communication 66(1):183-205 — porn consumption associated with sexual aggression (stronger for violent porn; correlational). Wright, Tokunaga, Kraus & Klann (2017), 'Pornography Consumption and Satisfaction: A Meta-Analysis,' Human Communication Research 43(3):315-343 — associated with lower relationship/sexual satisfaction in men (cross-sectional and longitudinal; weaker/null for women). Represents the 'effects are real' pole of the social-science debate.

entities.name: Christopher J. Ferguson, PhD
entities.covers: Stetson University psychologist; prominent skeptic of media-effects/moral-panic claims, including porn-aggression links.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Ferguson & Hartley (2022), 'Pornography and Sexual Aggression: Can Meta-Analysis Find a Link?' Trauma, Violence, & Abuse — re-examined the evidence and argued the porn-aggression link is weak, inconsistent, and possibly a statistical artifact; warns against moral-panic conclusions. Essential counterweight to Wright for an honest resource.

entities.name: Gary Wilson (1956-2021) / Your Brain on Porn
entities.covers: Late creator of the YourBrainOnPorn website and the viral TEDx talk 'The Great Porn Experiment' (2012). Popularized the 'supernormal stimulus/rebooting' model; major intellectual influence on NoFap.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Book 'Your Brain on Porn' (2014). Key paper: Park, Wilson et al. (2016), 'Is Internet Pornography Causing Sexual Dysfunctions? A Review with Clinical Reports,' Behavioral Sciences 6(3):17. CRITIQUES an honest resource must include: Wilson was not a credentialed neuroscientist (taught anatomy/physiology) and published no peer-reviewed primary experiments; the 2016 paper relied on case reports/anecdote and several authors had anti-porn advocacy ties; critics (Prause, Ley) say YBOP cherry-picked and overstated findings. Represents the popular/advocacy addiction model that drove public belief but outran the evidence.

entities.name: AASECT (American Association of Sexuality Educators, Counselors and Therapists)
entities.covers: Major US professional body for sexuality educators/therapists. Issued the most-cited skeptical institutional position on sex/porn addiction.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED 2016 position statement (exact language): AASECT 'does not find sufficient empirical evidence to support the classification of sex addiction or porn addiction as a mental health disorder' and 'does not find the sexual addiction training and treatment methods and educational pedagogies to be adequately informed by accurate human sexuality knowledge'; therefore linking problems to a 'porn/sexual addiction process cannot be advanced by AASECT as a standard of practice.' A pivotal, quotable institutional fact.

entities.name: World Health Organization — ICD-11 / CSBD (code 6C72)
entities.covers: WHO classification that created Compulsive Sexual Behaviour Disorder, the closest thing to official recognition.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: CSBD entered into force with ICD-11 on Jan 1, 2022, classified as an IMPULSE-CONTROL disorder (6C72), deliberately NOT placed with 'disorders due to addictive behaviours' (where gambling/gaming sit) because the working group found insufficient evidence for an addiction classification. Diagnostic guidelines explicitly state distress entirely due to moral judgments/disapproval is NOT sufficient for diagnosis (directly answering Grubbs's moral-incongruence concern). 'Problematic pornography use' is diagnosable under CSBD when full criteria (6+ months, impaired control, marked distress/impairment) are met. Foundational description: Kraus et al. 2018, World Psychiatry.

entities.name: SASH (Society for the Advancement of Sexual Health)
entities.covers: US organization (formerly National Council on Sexual Addiction and Compulsivity) representing the pro-treatment/compulsivity-and-addiction clinical camp.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Holds that compulsive/problematic sexual behavior is real and treatable; aligned with the addiction/compulsivity treatment tradition. Represents the institutional counterpoint to AASECT. An honest resource should present SASH and AASECT as the two institutional poles of the US debate.

entities.name: IITAP (International Institute for Trauma and Addiction Professionals)
entities.covers: Training body founded by Patrick Carnes; issues the CSAT (Certified Sex Addiction Therapist) credential.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Patrick Carnes ('Out of the Shadows,' 1983) popularized the modern 'sex addiction' concept and 30-task recovery model. IITAP/CSAT is the main credentialing arm of the sex-addiction treatment industry. Worth representing factually (with the caveat that AASECT and the DSM-5 declined to endorse the addiction model) so readers can evaluate provider credentials critically.

entities.name: Bowling Green / akjournals — International Sex Survey (Bothe et al.)
entities.covers: The largest multinational dataset on CSBD/problematic porn use, led by Beata Bothe and colleagues across 42 countries.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: International Sex Survey (Bothe et al., 2023, Journal of Behavioral Addictions) assessed CSBD/problematic porn use across 42 countries — a landmark for cross-cultural prevalence and the validation of screening tools (e.g., CSBD-19, PPCS) internationally. Use as the go-to current citation for global prevalence and instrument validity, noting rates vary widely by country/gender.

entities.name: University of Minnesota — Institute for Sexual and Gender Health (Eli Coleman)
entities.covers: Major US research center on compulsive sexual behavior; source of the most-cited US prevalence figure.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Dickenson, Gleason, Coleman & Miner (2018), 'Prevalence of Distress Associated With Difficulty Controlling Sexual Urges, Feelings, and Behaviors in the United States,' JAMA Network Open 1(7):e184468 — nationally representative sample (N=2,325): 8.6% reported clinically relevant distress/impairment (10.3% of men, 7.0% of women). This is the single best hard US prevalence statistic to cite.

entities.name: Common Sense Media
entities.covers: Credible US nonprofit research org; published the leading recent data on adolescent porn exposure.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: 'Teens and Pornography' (2023), nationally representative US survey of 13-17 year-olds: average age of first exposure ~12; 73% had seen online porn; 54% by age 13; 15% first saw it at age 10 or younger; 58% encountered it accidentally; a substantial share reported seeing aggressive/violent depictions. Best current citable hard statistics on youth exposure — directly relevant to the for-parents/for-educators audience and the prevention case.

entities.name: The Kinsey Institute (Indiana University)
entities.covers: Historic sex-research institute; relevant context for the academic study of sexuality and the porn-effects debate (home institution of Wright and other communication/sex researchers).
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: A leading academic hub for sexuality research; useful as an authoritative, non-ideological institutional anchor. Note for accuracy: many prominent CSBD researchers sit elsewhere (Minnesota, UNLV, Cambridge, Duisburg-Essen), so cite Kinsey for general sex-science credibility rather than as the CSBD-debate epicenter.

recommended_additions: Moral Incongruence & Self-Perceived Porn Addiction (net-new) — A dedicated deep-dive on Grubbs's PPMI two-pathway model, the religiosity/shame finding, and why self-labeled 'addiction' often is not clinical addiction. Currently only mentioned in passing on the-science and nofap-science; it is the most important single framework in the field and deserves its own page. Complements the-science and for-clinicians.

Prevalence & Epidemiology (net-new) — Consolidate the hard numbers in one citable place: Dickenson 2018 JAMA (8.6%; 10.3% men/7.0% women), the International Sex Survey 42-country data (Bothe 2023), self-perceived vs. clinical-threshold gap, and instrument-dependence caveat. No standalone epidemiology page exists; complements addiction-science and diagnostic-tools.

Porn-Induced Erectile Dysfunction (PIED): What the Evidence Shows (net-new) — Honest treatment of a hugely searched, contested claim: Park/Wilson 2016 clinical reports vs. Grubbs & Gola 2019 (no robust longitudinal link) and Landripet & Stulhofer 2015; distinguish performance anxiety/conditioning in a subset from a population 'epidemic.' PIED currently appears only on research-feed/porn-industry; deserves its own page and complements brain-science and for-clinicians.

Pornography, Relationships & Sexual Aggression (net-new) — Wright's satisfaction (2017) and aggression (2016) meta-analyses vs. Ferguson & Hartley (2022) rebuttal; present effect sizes and the causality caveat honestly. No page currently covers relational/aggression effects; complements the-science and for-parents.

The DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 Story (section to add to the-science or behavioral-addictions) — Make explicit the pivotal contrast: APA rejected Hypersexual Disorder from DSM-5 in 2013 (Reid field trial despite good psychometrics) while WHO added CSBD as an impulse-control (not addiction) disorder in ICD-11 (2022). This precise institutional history is currently only implicit.

Adolescents & Early Exposure (net-new or expand for-parents) — Center the 2023 Common Sense Media statistics (avg first exposure ~12; 15% by age 10; 58% accidental) as the evidence base for prevention; complements for-parents and prevention-programs.

How to Evaluate Porn-Science Claims (expand the existing 'How to read a study' section into a standalone media-literacy page) — Cross-sectional vs. longitudinal vs. experimental, correlation vs. causation, advocacy conflicts of interest (both anti-porn and industry), and why 'a study found' is not enough. The debate is uniquely polluted by motivated reasoning on both sides; a dedicated page is a differentiator.
findings.highest_value_gap: There is no dedicated, prominent page on moral incongruence and self-perceived porn addiction (Grubbs's PPMI model) — the single most important, most-replicated empirical finding in this literature: that self-labeled 'porn addiction' is driven substantially by religiosity/moral disapproval and shame, often more than by actual frequency of use, and that the ICD-11 explicitly excludes moral-distress-only cases from CSBD. For a resource that claims to be honest and non-ideological, this is the load-bearing concept that separates credible public-health framing from moral-panic framing; it is currently only mentioned in passing rather than given the standalone, deeply-cited treatment it warrants.

entities.name: Society for the Advancement of Sexual Health (SASH)
entities.covers: Professional/clinical body for compulsive sexual behavior; runs a clinician directory and annual conference; bridges the clinical field that historically used the 'sex addiction' frame.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: SASH maintains one of the few public clinician-finder directories specifically for compulsive sexual behavior. Worth folding in as a referral resource, while being explicit that the 'sex addiction' framing it grew out of is contested and NOT in DSM-5-TR (which has no porn/sex addiction diagnosis); ICD-11 instead lists Compulsive Sexual Behaviour Disorder (CSBD, code 6C72) as an impulse-control disorder, not an addiction. This diagnostic nuance is the single biggest thing most recovery sites get wrong.

entities.name: International Institute for Trauma & Addiction Professionals (IITAP) / CSAT certification
entities.covers: Trains and certifies Certified Sex Addiction Therapists (CSAT), the dominant clinician credential in the 'sex addiction' treatment world; founded around Patrick Carnes's model.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: CSAT is the credential most clinician-finders surface, but it is a proprietary certification, not a state license or an evidence-graded credential. A balanced page should explain what CSAT is, distinguish it from licensure (LMFT/LPC/LCSW/psychologist), and note the model's tasks/30-task framework lacks the RCT evidence base that CBT/ACT have. Citation/verification of current certificate counts needed via live source.

entities.name: Sex Addicts Anonymous (SAA)
entities.covers: Largest 12-step fellowship for compulsive sexual behavior; free, peer-led, worldwide meetings (in-person/phone/online); uses a member-defined 'sexual sobriety' / three-circles plan.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: SAA's 'three circles' (inner=bottom-line behaviors to avoid, middle=warning signs, outer=healthy activities) is a concrete, individualized harm-reduction tool worth explaining. Key honest caveat for our site: 12-step approaches for sexual behavior have very limited controlled-trial evidence (unlike AA for alcohol, the sexual-behavior fellowships are under-studied); they are accessible and free but not 'evidence-based' in the RCT sense. Distinguish SAA from SA below.

entities.name: Sexaholics Anonymous (SA)
entities.covers: 12-step fellowship with a SINGLE fixed sobriety definition (no sex outside heterosexual marriage; no masturbation).
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: SA is theologically/normatively stricter than SAA and its fixed sobriety definition has been criticized as exclusionary of LGBTQ+ and single people. Our site should contrast SA's fixed definition against SAA/SLAA member-defined sobriety so readers can choose a fellowship that fits their values rather than assuming all 12-step groups are interchangeable.

entities.name: Sex and Love Addicts Anonymous (SLAA)
entities.covers: 12-step fellowship addressing both compulsive sexual behavior AND love/relationship/romance compulsivity ('anorexia' and intrigue).
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: SLAA uniquely covers the love/romance/attachment dimension and 'sexual & emotional anorexia,' which the porn-focused literature often ignores. Useful for readers whose pattern is relational, not just porn use. Same evidence caveat as other fellowships.

entities.name: SMART Recovery
entities.covers: Secular, science-informed mutual-help program based on CBT/REBT and motivational tools; free meetings online and in person; explicitly an alternative to 12-step.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: SMART's 4-Point Program (build motivation, cope with urges, manage thoughts/feelings/behaviors, live a balanced life) and tools like the CBA (cost-benefit analysis), ABC (REBT), DISARM, and urge-surfing are directly applicable to porn/CSB and map onto the CBT/ACT evidence base. Critical gap to fill: SMART is the leading SECULAR option, important for the large share of strugglers alienated by 12-step's higher-power language or by faith-based programs like NoFap-adjacent communities. SMART has tools usable for any addictive behavior, not just substances.

entities.name: Refuge Recovery / Recovery Dharma
entities.covers: Buddhist/mindfulness-based, secular peer recovery framework for addictive behaviors generally.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Provides a mindfulness- and meditation-grounded peer alternative for people who want neither 12-step nor a purely clinical route. Aligns with the mindfulness/urge-surfing evidence (e.g., Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention concepts). Good to list as a secular, contemplative option distinct from SMART's CBT framing.

entities.name: Patrick Carnes, PhD
entities.covers: Originator of the modern clinical 'sex addiction' model, the 30-task recovery model, and the PATHOS/SAST screening instruments; founder figure behind CSAT/IITAP.
