entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Carnes is the most-cited name in the applied 'sex addiction' field and authored widely used screeners (SAST, SAST-R, PATHOS). For our site: cite him as historically foundational while being explicit that his addiction model is theory- and clinical-experience-driven and was NOT adopted by DSM-5; the diagnostic field moved toward ICD-11 CSBD instead. Exact publication years/instrument citations need live verification.

entities.name: Joshua Grubbs, PhD
entities.covers: Leading contemporary researcher on problematic pornography use; developed/validated key self-report measures and the influential 'moral incongruence' line of research.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Grubbs's work shows that self-reported 'porn addiction' is frequently driven by moral incongruence (using porn that conflicts with one's values/religious beliefs) rather than by objective frequency/severity — a finding with major treatment implications: for some, the distress is values-conflict, not a substance-like addiction, and ACT/values work or shame reduction may help more than abstinence-only framing. He is associated with the CPUI-9 (Cyber-Pornography Use Inventory) and the PPCS (Problematic Pornography Consumption Scale, the latter often attributed to Bőthe et al.). This 'moral incongruence vs. dysregulation' distinction is the most important nuance our recovery pages should teach. Verify exact citations/years via live source.

entities.name: Beáta Bőthe, PhD
entities.covers: Researcher behind the Problematic Pornography Consumption Scale (PPCS) and large-scale studies on porn use patterns and treatment-seeking.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: The PPCS operationalizes problematic use across six components (salience, mood modification, conflict, tolerance, relapse, withdrawal). Useful to fold into a 'how problematic use is actually measured' section that complements our diagnostic-tools page. Exact year/citation needs live verification.

entities.name: Michael Twohig, PhD (ACT for pornography research)
entities.covers: Clinical researcher who conducted some of the earliest controlled work applying Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) to problematic internet pornography viewing.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: ACT-for-pornography pilot/controlled studies reported meaningful reductions in viewing and in associated distress, making ACT one of the better-supported psychotherapeutic approaches for this specific behavior (alongside CBT). The mechanism — increasing psychological flexibility and values-based action rather than thought suppression — is a strong fit for moral-incongruence cases. IMPORTANT: present effect sizes only after live-source verification; do not cite specific numbers unverified.

entities.name: ICD-11 Compulsive Sexual Behaviour Disorder (CSBD) — WHO
entities.covers: The only current official diagnostic category covering this presentation; classified under impulse-control disorders (6C72), NOT as an addiction or substance-use disorder.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: CSBD's official criteria (persistent failure to control intense, repetitive sexual impulses/urges resulting in repetitive behavior over ≥6 months, marked distress/impairment, and an explicit exclusion that distress arising solely from moral judgment/disapproval does NOT qualify) should anchor any honest recovery page. The moral-judgment exclusion directly connects to Grubbs's moral-incongruence work. This is the authoritative, citable backbone our recovery-programs content should be built on.

entities.name: Psychology Today Therapist Finder
entities.covers: Largest general clinician-finder; filterable by specialty (sex therapy, addiction, CSAT), insurance, location, telehealth.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: This is where most people actually find a therapist. Our 'find a clinician' guidance should teach readers how to filter and vet (look for licensed clinicians, ask about ICD-11 CSBD/evidence-based modalities, be cautious of abstinence-only or shame-based framing) rather than just listing it. Pair with AASECT (below) for vetting sex-positive, ethically trained providers.

entities.name: AASECT (American Association of Sexuality Educators, Counselors and Therapists)
entities.covers: Certifies sex therapists and maintains a referral directory; sex-positive, ethics-forward orientation.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: AASECT notably issued a position declining to endorse 'sex addiction'/'porn addiction' as it lacks empirical support, instead favoring evidence-based assessment of sexual health concerns. Folding this in lets our site present BOTH camps honestly: the addiction-model providers (CSAT/SASH) and the sexual-health/sex-positive providers (AASECT) — and explain how a reader's beliefs and goals should guide which they choose. This balance is a real differentiator vs. most recovery sites that present only one camp.

entities.name: EMDR International Association (EMDRIA)
entities.covers: Credentialing body and therapist directory for EMDR; relevant because trauma frequently underlies compulsive sexual behavior.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: EMDR has a strong evidence base for PTSD but only indirect/limited evidence for compulsive sexual behavior specifically; it is best framed as treating underlying trauma drivers rather than the behavior itself. Our existing /emdr page should be cross-linked here with that honest scope caveat. EMDRIA's directory is the citable way to find a properly trained EMDR clinician.

recommended_additions: 'Does the treatment actually work? An evidence-grading guide' — net-new. Rank approaches by evidence quality (CBT and ACT: best-supported psychotherapies for problematic porn use; mindfulness/MBRP: promising; medication e.g. naltrexone/SSRIs: limited, mostly case-series/off-label; 12-step fellowships: accessible but under-studied for sexual behavior). Complements recovery-programs and treatment-modalities by adding an honest evidence hierarchy most sites omit.

'Secular and non-12-step recovery options' — complements peer-support-recovery. Covers SMART Recovery (CBT/REBT 4-Point Program), Recovery Dharma, and self-directed CBT/ACT, for the large audience alienated by higher-power or faith-based framing.

'Moral incongruence vs. genuine dysregulation: which one are you dealing with?' — net-new flagship explainer built on Grubbs's research and the ICD-11 moral-judgment exclusion. Teaches that for some people distress is a values conflict (better served by values/shame work) versus genuine loss of control — changing what 'recovery' should even target. This is the single highest-leverage page in the domain.

'How to find and vet a clinician' — complements get-help and for-clinicians. Explains CSAT vs. licensure vs. AASECT certification, the addiction-model vs. sexual-health-model split, what questions to ask, red flags (shame-based/abstinence-only-only), and how to use Psychology Today / AASECT / EMDRIA / SASH directories.

'12-step for sexual behavior, compared' — complements peer-support-recovery and hope-program. A side-by-side of SAA (member-defined sobriety, three circles), SA (single fixed definition), and SLAA (adds love/romance/attachment), with the honest evidence caveat and LGBTQ+/inclusivity notes.

'Relapse, lapse, and what the science says about urges' — complements addiction-science and recovery-programs. Teaches urge-surfing, the abstinence-violation effect, and that a lapse is not failure — reframing the all-or-nothing 'streak' culture (relevant given our nofap-science page).

'Medication and the brain: what's actually prescribed (and the thin evidence)' — complements brain-science and treatment-modalities. Covers off-label naltrexone, SSRIs (and their paradoxical use to dampen libido/compulsivity), and treatment of co-occurring conditions, with explicit 'this is low-evidence / talk to a prescriber' framing.
findings.highest_value_gap: An honest, evidence-graded treatment hierarchy paired with the 'moral incongruence vs. genuine behavioral dysregulation' distinction. Most recovery sites present a single ideology (either abstinence/12-step 'sex addiction' OR sex-positive dismissal) and imply one path fits everyone. The most authoritative thing digitalharm.org can add is: (1) anchor on the real diagnostic status (ICD-11 CSBD, an impulse-control disorder with an explicit moral-distress exclusion; no DSM-5-TR porn/sex addiction diagnosis); (2) grade the approaches by actual evidence (CBT/ACT best-supported, mindfulness promising, medication thin/off-label, 12-step accessible-but-under-studied for sexual behavior specifically); and (3) help the reader self-route based on whether their distress is values-conflict or loss-of-control. NOTE: before publishing, every specific statistic, study author, year, and effect size must be verified against live primary sources — live web retrieval was unavailable in this research session, so the entities above carry honest authority flags and several intentionally have empty URLs rather than guessed ones.

entities.name: National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC)
entities.covers: The US clearinghouse for child exploitation. Operates the CyberTipline (the legally mandated reporting channel for ESPs), Take It Down (free hash-based removal of minors' nude images), and publishes the single most-cited CSAM dataset in the world.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: CyberTipline received 20.5M reports in 2024 (down from 36.2M in 2023, but with a 192% jump in online enticement/sextortion to 546,000 reports and ~67,000 generative-AI reports, a ~1,325% increase YoY). Take It Down (takeitdown.ncmec.org) lets anyone who was under 18 in an image submit a hash to remove it across participating platforms without uploading the image itself. Our report-csam and ai-csam-response pages MUST link CyberTipline and Take It Down by name as the canonical actions and cite these exact 2024 figures with the source/year.

entities.name: Thorn (and its NoFiltr youth program)
entities.covers: Tech-driven anti-CSAM nonprofit. Builds detection tooling (Safer), runs the leading research library on generative-AI CSAM and youth attitudes, and runs NoFiltr (nofiltr.org), a youth-facing brand for sextortion/NCII support.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Led the 2024 'Safety by Design for Generative AI' principles, co-authored with All Tech Is Human and signed by Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Stability AI. Their research frames the AI-CSAM threat model (revictimization via fine-tuning on known victims, detection evasion by novel content). Our ai-csam-response and for-tech-ceos/for-developers pages should cite Thorn's Safety-by-Design framework and link the signatory list; NoFiltr should be in for-victims as a youth-voice support resource alongside Take It Down.

entities.name: WeProtect Global Alliance
entities.covers: 200+ member global policy alliance (governments, companies, civil society). Publishes the biennial Global Threat Assessment, the authoritative macro-statistics document for online child sexual exploitation worldwide.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Global Threat Assessment 2023: 32 million reports of suspected child sexual exploitation in 2022 (to NCMEC), an 87% increase since 2019; flags sharp rises in financial sextortion targeting teenage boys, generative-AI CSAM, and the detection risk from end-to-end encryption. These are the single best 'scale of the problem' citations for our international-resources, abuse-prevention-resources, and ai-csam-response pages. Always cite as 'WeProtect Global Threat Assessment 2023' with the year of the underlying data (2022).

entities.name: Internet Watch Foundation (IWF)
entities.covers: UK hotline that finds, assesses and removes CSAM webpages globally. Produces the most granular annual breakdown of CSAM by severity, age, and self-generated content, and pioneered reporting on AI-generated CSAM.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: IWF 2023 Annual Report: assessed 392,665 reports; confirmed 275,652 webpages containing CSAM or links to it (up from 255,580 in 2022). Self-generated imagery = 92% of actioned webpages (~254,070). Category A (most severe) appeared in 40,638 reports. Children aged 7-10 appeared on 106,176 webpages, a 68% rise YoY. IWF was first to document AI-CSAM proliferating on the dark web. These exact figures belong on abuse-prevention-resources, the-science, and ai-csam-response. Note the distinction: IWF counts webpages, NCMEC counts reports/files — explaining that difference is itself a trust signal.

entities.name: Lucy Faithfull Foundation / Stop It Now UK
entities.covers: The world's leading PERPETRATION-PREVENTION resource. A confidential, anonymous helpline and self-help tools (e.g. 'Get Help' / Shore) for people worried about their own sexual thoughts toward children or their viewing of illegal images — the demand-side intervention almost no US resource offers.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: This is the model for our for-offenders page and a likely net-new 'before you offend / concerned about your own behaviour' pathway. The Foundation works with the whole family system and with people at risk of offending. There is a US analogue (Stop It Now USA, stopitnow.org, 1-888-773-8368) and the academic Prevention Project Dunkelfeld in Germany. Our for-offenders/abuse-prevention pages should foreground anonymous help-seeking BEFORE harm as a recognized public-health strategy and link these helplines with numbers.

entities.name: Brave Movement
entities.covers: Survivor-led global advocacy movement to end childhood sexual violence; mobilizes survivors and allies to push governments and institutions for prevention and accountability.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Co-founded by Daniela Ligiero (also CEO of Together for Girls). Provides the survivor-VOICE and policy-advocacy dimension that org clearinghouses lack. Our for-victims and abuse-prevention-resources pages can link Brave Movement as the survivor-advocacy home, and cite the survivor-centered framing (centering lived experience, not just clinical/law-enforcement framing) as a trust differentiator.

entities.name: RAINN (Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network)
entities.covers: Largest US anti-sexual-violence org; runs the National Sexual Assault Hotline (800-656-HOPE) and the most-cited, well-sourced US child-sexual-abuse statistics page.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: RAINN's sourced stats: 1 in 9 girls and 1 in 20 boys under 18 experience sexual abuse/assault (Finkelhor et al., 2014, J. Adolescent Health); 93% of child victims know the perpetrator (34% family, 59% acquaintance, 7% stranger — BJS 2000); children most vulnerable ages 7-13. These specific, attributed figures should anchor our for-victims, crisis-resources and abuse-prevention pages — and model the citation style (named study + year) we should use everywhere.

entities.name: NSPCC / Childline
entities.covers: UK children's charity; runs Childline (counseling for children) and NSPCC Learning, which publishes rigorous statistics briefings on child sexual abuse and online safety for professionals.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: NSPCC Learning's 'Statistics briefing: child sexual abuse' is a professionally-curated, regularly-updated evidence summary — a model for what our for-clinicians/for-educators evidence sections should look like (clearly dated, source-linked). Childline is the UK youth-counseling analogue for our international-resources crisis list.

entities.name: Common Sense Media
entities.covers: The most trusted mainstream/secular parent brand for media reviews, app/parental-control roundups, digital-citizenship curriculum, and original research on kids and media.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Their 2023 'Teens and Pornography' report (n=1,358, ages 13-17) is the gold-standard youth-exposure citation: average age of first exposure is 12; 15% first saw it at age 10 or younger; 54% had seen it by 13; 73% of teens have consumed porn; 58% of viewers first encountered it accidentally; 52% have seen violent/aggressive porn (rape, choking, pain); 45% said it gave 'helpful' info about sex. These exact figures belong on for-parents, for-educators, the-science and brain-science. Their secular, research-based stance is the credibility posture we should match.

entities.name: Internet Matters
entities.covers: UK not-for-profit, industry-backed; best-in-class step-by-step parental-control setup guides across every device/platform/app, age-specific advice, and free downloadable resources.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Their differentiator is exhaustive, screenshot-driven 'how to turn on controls' guides. Our for-parents and apps pages should either match this how-to depth or explicitly link Internet Matters as the deep technical setup reference, while we own the 'why/what's the evidence' layer. Industry funding is a mild bias to note.

entities.name: Protect Young Eyes
entities.covers: Founder Chris McKenna; detailed app/game/platform safety reviews from a child-safety lens, parent/church education, and policy advocacy (age verification, Congressional testimony).
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Strong, frequently-updated app-review database and active in legislative advocacy (e.g. age-verification, KOSA-era testimony). Leans toward a faith/church audience — a bias to acknowledge. Our apps and for-parents pages should cite their app reviews while keeping our own framing secular and evidence-first.

entities.name: Bark
entities.covers: AI-driven monitoring service (texts, email, social, search) that alerts parents to predators, self-harm, bullying, and explicit content; also sells filtering and a kids' phone/watch.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Commercial product, so its blog is partly marketing — but its threat education (sextortion, predator grooming scripts) is practical. Treat as a tool to evaluate neutrally in our apps page, with the conflict-of-interest noted. Our edge: independent, non-commercial comparison of monitoring tools rather than a vendor's own claims.

entities.name: Covenant Eyes
entities.covers: Accountability/filtering software (Screen Accountability model) for a primarily Christian audience; publishes the widely-shared but heavily-criticized 'Porn Stats' compilation.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Their 'Porn Stats' page is one of the most-cited and most-misleading sources online — many figures are outdated, decontextualized, or untraceable. This is a direct opportunity: a rigorously-sourced, dated, myth-busting stats page that explicitly corrects the bad numbers circulating from Covenant Eyes and similar compilations would instantly out-rank and out-trust them. Note their explicit Christian, accountability-partner framing as a bias.

entities.name: Fight the New Drug
entities.covers: The largest secular-branded anti-porn awareness brand (founded 2009); 'porn is harmful' campaigns, the 'Brain Heart World' docuseries, and the Fortify recovery program partnership.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Huge reach and slick content, but repeatedly criticized by scientists for overstating/cherry-picking research and for downplayed ties to LDS/Mormon founders despite a 'non-religious' claim (see Wikipedia and David Ley/Nicole Prause critiques). Our trust edge: cite the SAME topics but with balanced, peer-reviewed evidence and explicit acknowledgement of contested claims. We should NOT mirror their certainty; we should be the resource that says what the evidence does and does not support.

entities.name: Your Brain on Porn (Gary Wilson)
entities.covers: The foundational 'porn rewires your brain / reboot' resource and a large studies bibliography; originated much of the NoFap-era neuroscience narrative.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Founder Gary Wilson (d. 2021) was not a clinician/neuroscientist; the site's addiction/'reboot' claims are widely disputed and its study list is criticized as selectively presented. Our nofap-science and brain-science pages should engage this directly: explain which claims (dopamine, sensitization, 'reboot') have real support, which are extrapolated from substance-addiction analogies, and cite the skeptics. Being the page that honestly adjudicates YBOP's claims is a major differentiator.

entities.name: NoFap / r/pornfree communities
entities.covers: Peer-support abstinence communities (NoFap.com plus Reddit r/NoFap and r/pornfree) with very large memberships; experiential support, streak tracking, motivational culture.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Strength = scale and lived peer support; weakness = pseudoscience ('superpowers', 'flatline'), no clinical oversight, and occasional ideological/incel-adjacent fringes. Our peer-support-recovery and nofap-science pages should validate the genuine value of peer support while clearly separating evidence from folklore, and point to clinically-grounded alternatives (SMART Recovery, therapy) as complements.

entities.name: Culture Reframed
entities.covers: Secular nonprofit (founder Gail Dines) framing porn/hypersexualized media as a children's public-health issue; free research-informed programs for parents of tweens and teens to build resilience.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Public-health, non-moralizing framing is close to our intended posture and worth aligning with; founder Dines is a polarizing anti-porn scholar, so cite the programs/resources rather than the most contested rhetoric. Good model and partner-link for our for-parents 'building resilience' content.

entities.name: Fortify / Impact Suite
entities.covers: Digital recovery program for compulsive porn use (Impact Suite), combining education, tracking, and community; partnered with Fight the New Drug.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Most prominent 'science-based' recovery app, but outcome evidence is largely self-published, not independent peer-reviewed RCTs. Our recovery-programs and apps pages should evaluate it honestly (what's evidence-informed vs. proven) and contrast with established modalities (CBT, ACT, SMART Recovery) on our treatment-modalities page.

entities.name: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline / SAMHSA / Crisis Text Line
entities.covers: Core US crisis infrastructure: 988 Lifeline (call/text 988), SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-HELP, treatment referrals), and Crisis Text Line (text HOME to 741741).
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: These exact numbers must be present and prominent on crisis-resources and get-help (988; 1-800-662-4357; text HOME to 741741). For shame-driven users (porn/CSAM contexts) a visible, non-judgmental crisis pathway is both safety-critical and a trust signal. Pair with the offender-prevention helplines (Stop It Now) so no user-type hits a dead end.

entities.name: Academic 'porn science' literature (Grubbs, Kraus, Potenza, Bothe, Prause, Ley)
entities.covers: The peer-reviewed evidence base our science pages should rest on, including the ICD-11 Compulsive Sexual Behaviour Disorder framework and the skeptic/critic camp.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Key citable facts: ICD-11 (effective Jan 2022) classifies Compulsive Sexual Behaviour Disorder as an IMPULSE-CONTROL disorder, explicitly NOT an addiction; DSM-5 (2013) recognizes neither 'porn addiction', 'sex addiction', nor hypersexual disorder. Roughly 3-6% of adults report problematic porn use. Joshua Grubbs' 'moral incongruence' research shows self-labeled 'porn addiction' often tracks religiosity/moral conflict more than actual use frequency. Named researchers: Grubbs (moral incongruence), Kraus & Potenza (CSBD), Beata Bothe (measurement), Nicole Prause & David Ley (addiction-model skeptics), Rory Reid (hypersexual disorder). Our the-science, addiction-science, behavioral-addictions, brain-science and nofap-science pages should cite these names/findings and present BOTH sides — this scientific even-handedness is our single biggest trust advantage over every advocacy competitor.

recommended_additions: Add an outbound-citation/sources layer to EVERY existing page (net-new behavior) — the site currently cites almost no external authorities (a site-wide scan found only 3 mentions of NCMEC and ZERO mentions of Thorn, IWF, RAINN, WeProtect, Common Sense Media, NSPCC, Stop It Now, Covenant Eyes, FTND, YBOP, or NoFap). This is the highest-leverage fix: uncited claims read as unverifiable. Complements all pages.

'Porn statistics: what's true, what's myth' — a rigorously dated, source-linked stats page that corrects the widely-circulated bad numbers (esp. Covenant Eyes 'Porn Stats') and presents verified figures (Common Sense 2023 youth-exposure data, IWF 2023, NCMEC 2024, WeProtect 32M/87%). Net-new; complements the-science and porn-industry.

'Is porn addiction real? What the evidence actually says' — an honest adjudication of the ICD-11 CSBD vs DSM-5 debate, the 3-6% prevalence, and Grubbs' moral-incongruence finding, engaging YBOP/NoFap claims head-on. Complements nofap-science, behavioral-addictions, and addiction-science.

A 'Concerned about your own thoughts/behavior toward children?' anonymous-help pathway modeled on Stop It Now / Lucy Faithfull / Dunkelfeld — perpetration prevention is the biggest missing public-health lever. Complements/strengthens for-offenders and abuse-prevention-resources.
'Take It Down & removing intimate images' action page — step-by-step on NCMEC Take It Down, Thorn/NoFiltr, and StopNCII for sextortion/NCII victims. Complements for-victims and report-csam.

A transparent 'How we vet sources / editorial standards' page (named reviewers, dated reviews, conflict-of-interest disclosure, secular non-moralizing stance) — directly out-trusts advocacy competitors whose biases (religious, commercial, ideological) are undisclosed. Net-new; complements about.

An independent, non-commercial 'monitoring & filtering tools compared' guide (Bark, Covenant Eyes, Internet Matters guides, Protect Young Eyes reviews) with disclosed methodology — owns the neutral-comparison niche no vendor can. Complements apps and for-parents.
findings.highest_value_gap: The site's single biggest gap is credible, visible sourcing. A full-site scan shows it currently cites almost no external authorities (only 3 NCMEC mentions; zero for Thorn, IWF, RAINN, WeProtect, Common Sense Media, NSPCC, Stop It Now, and every recovery competitor). To be 'the world's most authoritative resource,' it must do the one thing every competitor fails at: pair each claim with a dated, named, peer-reviewed or primary-source citation AND honestly present scientific controversy (ICD-11 CSBD-as-impulse-control vs DSM-5 non-recognition; the 3-6% problematic-use prevalence; Grubbs' moral-incongruence finding). Advocacy sites (Fight the New Drug, Covenant Eyes, Your Brain on Porn, NoFap) win on reach but lose on trust because they overstate certainty and hide religious/commercial/ideological bias; clearinghouses (NCMEC, IWF, Thorn, WeProtect) win on authority but are fragmented and audience-specific. The unclaimed position is a single secular, transparently-sourced, even-handed meta-resource that adjudicates the evidence, corrects the bad statistics in circulation, links the right specialist org for each audience (including the near-absent perpetration-prevention pathway via Stop It Now/Lucy Faithfull), and discloses its own editorial standards.

entities.name: National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) - NetSmartz, KidSmartz, CyberTipline & Take It Down
entities.covers: NCMEC runs the U.S. national reporting mechanism (CyberTipline), the youth education programs NetSmartz (age-segmented K-2/3-5/6-8/9-12 curricula, videos, lesson plans, discussion guides on online safety, sextortion, grooming) and KidSmartz (K-5 abuse-prevention built on the '4 Rules of Personal Safety'), and Take It Down, the free hash-based service to remove minors' nude/sexual images from participating platforms.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED hard stats (NCMEC, all citable): CyberTipline received 36.2M reports in 2023 and 20.5M in 2024 (drop attributed to report bundling and Meta end-to-end encryption; adjusted = 29.2M incidents in 2024). Financial sextortion reports: 10,731 (2022), 26,718 (2023), 33,000+ (2024, +24%), about 100/day. Online enticement (category that includes sextortion): 546,000+ reports in 2024, +192% over 2023 (partly the 2024 REPORT Act). CyberTipline reports involving Generative AI rose 1,325% in 2024. NCMEC is aware of at least 36 teenage boys who died by suicide after sextortion since 2021. ACTION TO FOLD IN: Take It Down (takeitdown.ncmec.org) lets a minor (or adult who was a minor in the image) hash it on their OWN device so platforms block it without it ever being uploaded. KidSmartz '4 Rules': Check First, Take a Friend, Tell People No, Tell a Trusted Adult. Backbone U.S. reporting + removal pathway (CyberTipline.org / 1-800-843-5678).

entities.name: Thorn
entities.covers: Tech nonprofit building child-safety detection tools and publishing the most-cited recurring youth research: the annual 'Youth Perspectives on Online Safety' series, plus 'Trends in Financial Sextortion' (June 2024, with NCMEC) and 'Sexual Extortion & Young People' (June 2025). Runs Thorn for Parents.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED prevalence stats. Youth Perspectives on Online Safety, 2024 (pub. Sept 2025): 33% of boys aged 9-12 reported an online sexual interaction, highest since tracking began 2020 (sexual messages +12%, asked for nudes +9%); 1 in 3 reported being asked for sexual imagery before 18. HELP-SEEKING GAP: 1 in 5 (20%) minors who had an online sexual interaction told no one; only 60% of that group had a trusted adult; LGBTQ+ youth least likely of all (51%). 1 in 10 minors reshared someone else's nude without consent. Sextortion: 6% of minors 9-17 experienced it; 1 in 6 victims were 12 or younger at first experience; 1 in 7 sextortion victims were driven to self-harm (28% among LGBTQ+). Crisis text line: text THORN to 741741. Disclosure-safety finding supports a 'relationship before software / no matter what, you can come to me' framing.

entities.name: FBI & DHS/HSI - sextortion alerts and the Know2Protect campaign
entities.covers: U.S. federal lead on child sexual exploitation. FBI/HSI/NCMEC issued the national public-safety alert on financial sextortion; FBI runs 'Stop Sextortion'; DHS launched 'Know2Protect' (know2protect.gov) in April 2024, the first national campaign on online child sexual exploitation.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: VERIFIED figures plus the gold-standard victim script. FBI/HSI received 13,000+ financial-sextortion reports Oct 2021-March 2023, 12,600+ victims (mostly boys), at least 20 suicides; victims interviewed as young as 8-10; targets typically boys 14-17; offenders usually overseas (Nigeria, Ivory Coast, Philippines - 'Yahoo Boys'). DHS: online enticement reports jumped 292,951 to 518,720 (Jan-June 2024 vs 2025); GenAI-related CSE reports soared 6,835 to 440,419 same window. FBI VICTIM SCRIPT to fold in: (1) STOP contact; (2) DON'T pay/comply - paying does NOT stop it; (3) DON'T delete - preserve evidence; (4) BLOCK but screenshot usernames first; (5) REPORT to FBI (tips.fbi.gov / 1-800-CALL-FBI) + NCMEC CyberTipline, use Take It Down. Core message: the blackmailer is to blame, not the child; you are not in trouble. Know2Protect is the best one-stop U.S. hub.

entities.name: Protect Young Eyes
entities.covers: U.S. parent-focused digital-safety org (Chris McKenna, '5 Habits of the Tech-Ready Family,' 2026) known for regularly-updated device/app Parent Guides, parental-control walkthroughs, school talks, and a '5 Layers of Protection' framework (Relationships, WiFi/Router, Device, Location, App).
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Most actionable operational layer to link out to. VERIFIED free downloads our site lacks: 'What to Do' guides for 'My Kid Sent a Nude,' 'Received a Nude,' 'Is Being Sextorted,' 'Is Talking to a Predator'; Smartphone- and Social-Media-Readiness ('what age?') guides; a smartphone/tech agreement template; ebook 'My Kid Has Seen Porn. Now What?' Their 5 Layers leads with Layer 1: Relationships (build digital trust) before software. Their sextortion guide aggregates Network Contagion Research Institute data: about 93% of financial-sextortion victims are male, most 15-17, 51% via Instagram, 31% via Snapchat, summer peak. Concrete conversation entry points ('10 Before 10: Making Porn a Normal Conversation,' 'How to Talk to a 5-year-old About Porn'). Guides kept current, offloading maintenance our static page can't carry. Good complement to /apps.

entities.name: Common Sense Media
entities.covers: Major U.S. nonprofit: age-based media reviews, the free K-12 'Digital Citizenship Curriculum' (with Harvard Project Zero, widely adopted), and large-scale research (the 'Common Sense Census' and the 'Teens and Pornography' report).
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Two citable assets. (1) The free K-12 Digital Citizenship Curriculum - turnkey, standards-aligned (media balance, privacy, cyberbullying, digital footprint, news literacy) - ideal for /for-educators. (2) VERIFIED: Common Sense Media's 2022 'Teens and Pornography' report found 41% of teens reported seeing pornography during the school day and 44% of those reported viewing it on school-owned devices. Among the most citable U.S. figures on teen porn exposure; supports both a 'younger than curricula assume' framing and phone-free-school arguments. Also publishes a 'talk-along' sexting conversation resource and AI-literacy materials relevant to nudify/deepfake conversations.

entities.name: Internet Matters
entities.covers: Leading UK not-for-profit providing age-banded online-safety advice for parents and schools (0-5, 6-10, 11-13, 14+), platform/device parental-control setup guides, hubs on nudes/sexting, grooming, and pornography, plus 'Digital Matters' (free interactive lessons, ages 9-11). Publishes an annual children's-online-experiences tracker.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Best age-banded conversation scaffolding for /for-parents - concrete 'what to say at each age' plus printable conversation starters, and step-by-step parental-controls guides across broadband, mobile, consoles, apps. 'Digital Matters' is a free, citable school curriculum (ages 9-11). Research arm publishes UK tracker data on children's exposure to pornography/harmful content (cite current-year figures from internetmatters.org/research). Now publishes specific guidance on AI/'nudify' deepfake nudes for parents and schools. Authoritative, free, well-structured.

entities.name: Bark Technologies
entities.covers: Commercial AI monitoring service scanning texts, email, and 30+ apps for signs of sextortion, predators, self-harm, bullying, and explicit content; sells the Bark Phone/Watch; publishes an annual aggregate-detection report and a free parent blog.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Bark's annual detection data is a citable real-world signal of risk prevalence (cite current figures from bark.us/annual-report). For /apps, state the honest trade-off: monitoring can catch danger early but erodes trust if covert - best paired with transparency ('we use this, here's what it does/doesn't see'). List alongside non-monitoring options (Apple Screen Time, Google Family Link, Covenant Eyes for porn-specific filtering, router/DNS filtering). Free per-app explainers and 'what sextortion looks like' content are parent-friendly.

entities.name: UK Department for Education - statutory RSHE / RSE curriculum
entities.covers: England's statutory Relationships, Sex and Health Education framework. Relationships Education mandatory in primary, RSE in secondary (in force since Sept 2020), with required content on online relationships, consent, sharing of nudes, and the harms of pornography. ('PSHE' is the delivery subject; 'RSHE/RSE' is the statutory component.)
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: The most authoritative government-mandated curriculum framework for what schools are legally required to teach - policy backbone for /for-educators (UK/international). Secondary pupils must be taught that online pornography can present a distorted picture of sexual behaviours, the law on sharing nude images, and online grooming. NOTE: DfE consulted on and updated RSHE guidance in 2024-2025 (including age-appropriateness limits) - verify the current version at gov.uk before citing age thresholds. Complement with the PSHE Association programme of study (pshe-association.org.uk) and name the UK regulatory layer: Online Safety Act 2023 and Ofcom's child-safety/age-assurance codes.

entities.name: UK Safer Internet Centre / Childnet & SWGfL (incl. Report Remove)
entities.covers: UK Safer Internet Centre (Childnet + IWF + SWGfL): runs Safer Internet Day, free age-banded school education packs and assemblies, the Professionals Online Safety Helpline (POSH), and (with NSPCC/Childline) 'Report Remove,' the UK takedown route for under-18 nude images. Childnet also publishes toolkits on online sexual harassment and AI/deepfake nudes.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Childnet's free age-banded resources and assembly packs are turnkey for /for-educators. 'Report Remove' is the concrete UK image-removal action for under-18s (UK counterpart to NCMEC's Take It Down) - fold into /for-victims for a UK audience. Childnet's emerging-threat toolkits cover peer-on-peer deepfake nudes in schools, increasingly relevant 2024-2026.

entities.name: NSPCC / Childline - 'Talk PANTS' / Pantosaurus
entities.covers: UK's leading child-protection charity. Runs Childline (free under-19 helpline, 0800 1111), the early-years 'Talk PANTS' body-safety campaign (mascot Pantosaurus), parent online-safety advice, and 'Report Remove' with the IWF.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: PANTS is the best-known, easiest-to-adapt early-years (ages ~4-8) body-safety script and complements NCMEC KidSmartz: Privates are private; Always remember your body belongs to you; No means no; Talk about secrets that upset you; Speak up, someone can help. Fold the full acronym into a young-child section on /for-parents. Childline (0800 1111) and Report Remove are concrete UK action steps. NSPCC publishes clear age-appropriate conversation advice and (with O2) a parent online-safety helpline.

entities.name: Internet Watch Foundation (IWF)
entities.covers: UK hotline that finds, assesses, and removes child sexual abuse imagery; the principal global data source on the scale and nature of web-hosted CSAM, 'self-generated' imagery, and AI-generated CSAM.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: IWF annual reports are among the most citable hard-data sources on the CSAM problem itself (cite exact figures/year from iwf.org.uk/annual-report): record volumes of webpages containing CSAM, a dominant and rising share being 'self-generated' (often coerced over webcams in the child's own bedroom, with a sharp rise among 7-10 year-olds), more Category A (most severe) material, and a growing volume of AI-generated CSAM it now actively tracks. Use the 'self-generated in the child's own bedroom' finding to motivate concrete device-placement guidance for parents (no devices behind closed doors at night; charge phones outside bedrooms). Quantifies the scale claim for /abuse-prevention-resources and /report-csam.

entities.name: Take It Down (NCMEC) & StopNCII.org (SWGfL)
entities.covers: Two free hash-matching image-removal services: Take It Down (NCMEC) for images of minors (or images taken when the person was a minor); StopNCII.org (SWGfL) for adults 18+ facing non-consensual intimate image abuse. Both hash the image locally so the file is never uploaded.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: The two most concrete, empowering removal tools for /for-victims and any sextortion section - the distinction matters: under-18 imagery goes to Take It Down; adult/18+ imagery goes to StopNCII.org. Both create a hash on the user's own device and share only the hash with participating platforms (Meta, TikTok, Snap, Aylo/Pornhub, Bumble, OnlyFans, others) to detect and block matching uploads without anyone ever seeing the image. The U.S. TAKE IT DOWN Act (signed 2025) now legally requires covered platforms to remove reported NCII/CSAM quickly - a citable policy backstop. Our site does not yet surface these tools and should.

entities.name: Culture Reframed
entities.covers: U.S. nonprofit (Dr. Gail Dines) focused specifically on building youth resilience to hypersexualized media and online pornography. Offers a free 'Parents Program' (separate Tweens and Teens tracks) and a 'Program for Educators' - structured multi-module online courses.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: One of the few organizations whose curricula are built specifically around pornography (not generic online safety) with a public-health frame - directly on-mission for digitalharm.org. The free Parents Program (Tweens / Teens) and Educators Program are turnkey, citable courses to recommend on /for-parents and /for-educators. Emphasizes media literacy, critical analysis of porn's messages about gender and consent, and ongoing dialogue over one-time talks. Fills a clear gap: our pages discuss porn harm but don't point parents/educators to a porn-specific resilience curriculum.

entities.name: Wait Until 8th / Smartphone Free Childhood / Jonathan Haidt ('The Anxious Generation')
entities.covers: Grassroots 'delay the smartphone' movement (Wait Until 8th, US), the parallel UK parent movement Smartphone Free Childhood (founded 2024), and the research/advocacy popularized by Jonathan Haidt's 'The Anxious Generation' (2024) and his 4 norms.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: The most actionable collective-action framework for the 'before you hand over a phone' section. Wait Until 8th lets parents pledge to delay smartphones until at least 8th grade, activated once enough families in a grade join (solving 'but everyone else has one'). Haidt's 4 norms (2024): no smartphone before high school; no social media before 16; phone-free schools; more independent play - a clean, quotable scaffold. Treat Haidt's phone-to-mental-health causal claim carefully (debated among researchers; cite the framework, not as settled consensus). Australia's 2024 law setting a social-media minimum age of 16 is a citable parallel. Strong fit for /for-parents and phone-free-school policy on /for-educators.

entities.name: Be Internet Awesome (Google) / Interland
entities.covers: Google's free K-6 digital-citizenship curriculum (ISTE-aligned) built on five pillars (Smart, Alert, Strong, Kind, Brave) and the kid-facing game 'Interland.' Widely used in U.S. elementary schools.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Turnkey, free, gamified curriculum for younger students - list on /for-educators as a lighter complement to Common Sense and NetSmartz. Mnemonic: Be Internet Smart/Alert/Strong/Kind/Brave. Honest caveat for our audience: industry-produced (Google) and skews to general citizenship/privacy rather than pornography or grooming - pair with a porn/exploitation-specific program (NetSmartz, Culture Reframed).

entities.name: Defend Young Minds - 'Good Pictures Bad Pictures'
entities.covers: U.S. parent-resource company best known for the read-aloud book series 'Good Pictures Bad Pictures,' which gives young children a concrete plan for what to do when they see pornography, plus a parent blog and courses.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Provides the most widely-used concrete SCRIPT for the 'what do I do if I see a bad picture' conversation with young children - a simple, memorable plan (turn away / close the device, tell a trusted adult, understand in age-appropriate terms why porn is harmful). Exactly the actionable, copy-able framework our /for-parents page lacks for the under-10 band. Faith-friendly origin but the core 'install an internal filter, here's the step-by-step plan' approach is secular and broadly usable. Complements PANTS and KidSmartz for the youngest band.

entities.name: WeProtect Global Alliance
entities.covers: Global multi-stakeholder alliance (governments, companies, civil society) that publishes the biennial 'Global Threat Assessment' and topic briefings, including 'A web of deceit: Financial sexual extortion of children and young people' (June 2024).
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Authoritative international framing to round out a U.S./UK-heavy resource. WeProtect's 2024 'A web of deceit' briefing documents the global surge in financial sexual extortion of children - primarily teenage boys, often progressing from first message to coercion within hours - and links the trend to 20+ youth suicides (media-reported). Its Global Threat Assessment is the standard citation for the worldwide scale of online child sexual exploitation. Good fit for /international-resources and to source the 'this is global and fast-moving' point in any sextortion guide.

entities.name: eSafety Commissioner (Australia)
entities.covers: The world's first government online-safety regulator. Extensive age-based parent/educator resources, the 'eSafety Guide' to apps/games, a formal image-based-abuse reporting and takedown scheme, school programs ('Toolkit for Schools'), and youth-experience research.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: A model for citable, government-grade guidance with a working complaints/takedown scheme - reference on /international-resources and /for-parents. eSafety publishes age-banded advice, specific sextortion and image-based-abuse guidance with a legal reporting route (esafety.gov.au/report), and research on young Australians' exposure to pornography and harmful content (cite current figures from esafety.gov.au/research). Australia's late-2024 law setting a minimum social-media age of 16 is a citable 'delay access' policy data point.

recommended_additions: Sextortion: A Survival Guide - NET-NEW, highest priority. Complements /for-victims and /report-csam. Split financial sextortion (teen boys, money; 33,000+ NCMEC reports in 2024, about 100/day) from coercive image-based sextortion. Lead with the FBI/NCMEC response script (STOP contact, DON'T pay, DON'T delete/preserve evidence, BLOCK after screenshotting, REPORT to tips.fbi.gov + NCMEC CyberTipline) and the non-shaming message ('the blackmailer is to blame, not you; paying will not make it stop'), then the free removal tools (Take It Down for under-18; Report Remove UK; StopNCII for adults).

Build out /for-parents from stub - NET-NEW. (1) relationship-first framing (Thorn: 20% of kids who had an online sexual interaction told no one; only 60% had a trusted adult); (2) age-banded conversation scripts (Internet Matters 0-5/6-10/11-13/14+ plus NSPCC PANTS for under-8s plus 'Good Pictures Bad Pictures' plan); (3) the sextortion talk plus exact victim-response script; (4) device/filter setup linking to Protect Young Eyes + Bark with the trust trade-off stated; (5) 'before the first phone' (Wait Until 8th, Haidt's 4 norms, device-placement: no phones in bedrooms at night).

Build out /for-educators from stub - NET-NEW. The single highest-value addition is a non-shaming, step-by-step victim-and-parent playbook built on the authoritative FBI/NCMEC response script (do not pay, do not comply further, preserve evidence, block, report to NCMEC CyberTipline + FBI tips.fbi.gov) plus the free image-removal pathways (NCMEC Take It Down for minors; SWGfL Report Remove in the UK; StopNCII for adults). This is the query a terrified teen or parent types at 2am, and right now the site has nothing for them.

entities.name: NCMEC Take It Down
entities.covers: Free service from the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children that helps remove or stop the online spread of nude, partially nude, or sexually explicit images/videos of someone who was under 18 when the image was taken (or who is currently a minor).
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Critical mechanic to document: Take It Down is hash-based and privacy-preserving — the image/video NEVER leaves the user's device. The tool generates a cryptographic hash (digital fingerprint) on-device; only the hash is submitted to NCMEC, which shares it with participating platforms so they can detect and remove matching content. A minor (or a parent/trusted adult acting for them, or an adult who has imagery from when they were a minor) can use it anonymously without creating an account or reporting to police. Participating platforms have included Meta (Facebook/Instagram), Yubo, OnlyFans, Pornhub/MindGeek (Aylo), Snapchat, and others — verify current list at the site. Step-by-step path worth documenting: (1) locate the image/video on your own device, (2) go to takeitdown.ncmec.org, (3) select the platform(s) where it appears, (4) the tool hashes the file locally, (5) submit the hash, (6) participating platforms scan for matches and remove/block. Limitation to state plainly: it only works on participating platforms and only if the exact image hash matches; it cannot guarantee removal everywhere. Distinct from CyberTipline (which is for reporting offenders). Launched December 2022.

entities.name: StopNCII.org (operated by SWGfL / Revenge Porn Helpline)
entities.covers: Free hash-matching tool for ADULTS (18+) to prevent the non-consensual sharing of their intimate images (NCII), including AI-generated/deepfake and synthetic nude imagery. The adult counterpart to Take It Down.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Same privacy-preserving on-device hashing model — the intimate image is NOT uploaded; a hash is generated in the user's browser and only that hash is shared with industry partners. Eligibility: must be 18+ and the person in the image (under-18 cases route to NCMEC Take It Down). Now explicitly covers synthetic/deepfake intimate imagery. Industry partners to document include Meta (Facebook, Instagram, Threads), TikTok, Bumble, Reddit, Snap/Snapchat, OnlyFans, Pornhub/Aylo, Microsoft (Bing), and others — confirm current partner list on site. Operated by SWGfL, the UK charity that also runs the Revenge Porn Helpline. By 2024 StopNCII reported it had created hundreds of thousands of hashes and supported well over 100,000+ cases (verify latest figure on the site's stats page before publishing). Step-by-step: create a case on stopncii.org, select images from your device, the browser hashes them locally, receive a case number to track status. This is the single most important adult takedown tool to surface alongside Take It Down.

entities.name: Canadian Centre for Child Protection — Project Arachnid
entities.covers: Global web-crawler and takedown platform that detects known CSAM/CSEM across the open web and issues removal notices to electronic service providers; survivors can register imagery for proactive detection and removal.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Project Arachnid crawls the web and processes tens of thousands of images per second against known CSAM hashes. As of recent reporting it had detected/processed billions of images and issued well over 40 million takedown notices to electronic service providers worldwide (verify the latest cumulative figure on protectchildren.ca / projectarachnid.ca before publishing, as the number grows continuously). The Canadian Centre also operates Cybertip.ca (Canada's national tipline) and is the institutional home of survivor-led advocacy. Key survivor service to document: survivors can work with the Centre to have their abuse imagery proactively detected and removed, and the Centre publishes survivor-impact research (e.g., its 'Survivors' Survey' / 'International Survivors' Survey' documenting the ongoing trauma of imagery recirculation). This is the leading non-US takedown infrastructure and complements NCMEC tools.

entities.name: The Phoenix 11
entities.covers: A group of survivors whose child sexual abuse was recorded and, in most cases, distributed online, who have joined together to advocate for stronger responses to CSAM. Co-convened by the Canadian Centre for Child Protection and (historically) the Canadian and US-based survivor support efforts.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: The Phoenix 11 is the most prominent organized survivor-advocacy group specific to CSAM (as distinct from general sexual-assault survivor groups). They speak publicly (often anonymously/with identity protection) about the unique harm of CSAM: that the crime is permanent and re-perpetrated every time imagery is viewed or shared. They have testified to legislators and pushed platforms and governments for proactive detection and removal. Worth documenting as proof that an organized survivor community exists and as a model for survivor-centered policy advocacy. Related survivor groups to mention: the 'Chicago Males' survivor group and survivor advocates organized through Marsh Law / the National Center for Victims of Crime. Frame for the for-victims page: survivors are not alone and there are peer-advocacy communities specifically for image-based child abuse.

entities.name: Marsh Law Firm (CSAM survivor litigation)
entities.covers: US law firm specializing in civil litigation and restitution for survivors of child sexual abuse material, representing many of the survivors known in restitution case law (e.g., 'Amy,' 'Vicky,' 'Andy').
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Marsh Law (attorneys including James Marsh and Margaret Mabie) pioneered using 18 U.S.C. § 2255 ('Masha's Law') and federal restitution statutes to recover monetary damages for CSAM survivors from offenders who possess/distribute their imagery. They operate childvictim.com as a survivor-facing resource. Document the practical path: a survivor whose imagery is in known NCMEC series can register to receive victim notifications when their images appear in new prosecutions and can seek restitution in each case. Carol L. Hepburn is another key survivor-restitution attorney (represents 'Vicky'). These firms are the bridge between the criminal-justice system and survivor financial recovery. Important for the for-victims and for-attorneys pages: restitution and § 2255 civil claims are concrete, underused remedies.

entities.name: Masha's Law (18 U.S.C. § 2255) and Paroline v. United States
entities.covers: The US federal civil-remedy and restitution legal landscape for CSAM survivors: statutory minimum damages and the mandatory restitution framework.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Hard legal facts to document precisely: (1) 18 U.S.C. § 2255 ('Masha's Law'), as amended by the Amy, Vicky, and Andy Child Pornography Victim Assistance Act of 2018 (AVAA), provides a federal civil cause of action with statutory liquidated damages of no less than $150,000 per defendant for survivors of child sexual exploitation. (2) Paroline v. United States, 572 U.S. 434 (2014) — the Supreme Court held that a CSAM possessor owes restitution to a victim, but only for the portion of the victim's losses proximately caused by that defendant, rejecting both full aggregate liability and zero liability. (3) The AVAA (2018) responded to Paroline by creating, among other things, a minimum restitution amount of $3,000 for trafficking-in-child-pornography offenses and establishing the Child Pornography Victims Reserve (a DOJ fund) so survivors can elect 'defined monetary assistance' (a one-time payment, capped — historically $35,000, adjusted for inflation) instead of pursuing each defendant individually. Cite the statute years and the case citation exactly. This is the backbone of the restitution section for both for-victims and for-attorneys.

entities.name: DOJ Child Pornography Victims Reserve / AVAA defined monetary assistance
entities.covers: Federal fund administered by DOJ allowing eligible CSAM survivors to receive a one-time 'defined monetary assistance' payment without litigating against individual offenders.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Created by the Amy, Vicky, and Andy Child Pornography Victim Assistance Act of 2018. A survivor whose imagery is part of an identified series in the NCMEC Child Victim Identification Program can apply once for a lump-sum payment from the Reserve (the statutory base figure is $35,000, subject to inflation adjustment) as an alternative to seeking restitution defendant-by-defendant. Funded through assessments on convicted offenders. Document the eligibility path and that survivors can choose EITHER defined monetary assistance OR case-by-case restitution. This is a concrete, low-friction remedy many survivors don't know exists — high value for the for-victims page. Verify the current inflation-adjusted amount and application process on justice.gov before publishing.

entities.name: TAKE IT DOWN Act (Pub. L. 119-12, 2025)
entities.covers: Federal US law criminalizing the publication of non-consensual intimate imagery (including AI-generated deepfakes) and requiring covered online platforms to remove such content on victim request.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Hard facts to document: The TAKE IT DOWN Act (S.146, 119th Congress) was signed into law by President Trump on May 19, 2025. It (1) makes it a federal crime to knowingly publish, or threaten to publish, non-consensual intimate images of adults or minors, explicitly including AI-generated/'digital forgery' deepfake imagery; and (2) requires covered platforms to establish a notice-and-removal process and to remove reported NCII within 48 HOURS of a valid victim request (and make reasonable efforts to remove copies). The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) enforces the removal requirement, treating violations as unfair/deceptive practices. Platforms had roughly ONE YEAR from enactment to stand up compliant removal systems (i.e., by approximately May 2026). Sponsors included Senators Ted Cruz and Amy Klobuchar; First Lady Melania Trump championed it. This is the most important recent legal development for victims — document the 48-hour removal right and the FTC complaint avenue as a concrete action victims can take.

entities.name: Cyber Civil Rights Initiative (CCRI) Crisis Helpline & Safety Center
entities.covers: Nonprofit dedicated to combating non-consensual intimate imagery; operates a free, confidential image-abuse crisis helpline and an online Safety Center with removal guides.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: CCRI runs a free, confidential Image Abuse Crisis Helpline at 1-844-878-2274 (1-844-878-CCRI) serving victims of NCII, sextortion, and deepfake abuse. It also maintains the CCRI Safety Center with platform-specific content-removal guides, an 'Online Removal Guide,' and information on legal options and state laws. CCRI was founded by Dr. Mary Anne Franks and Holly Jacobs and was instrumental in drafting model NCII legislation. Document the helpline number, that it's free/confidential, and the platform-by-platform removal guides as a practical victim resource. CCRI is also a leading source of US state-law tracking (which states criminalize NCII/deepfakes).

entities.name: NCMEC CyberTipline & Child Victim Identification Program (CVIP)
entities.covers: The US national mechanism for reporting online child sexual exploitation, and the program that identifies victims in CSAM and connects identified survivors to victim notification and restitution.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Hard stats to document (verify latest year on missingkids.org before publishing): the CyberTipline received more than 36 million reports in 2023 and over 20 million reports in 2024 (the apparent drop reflects reporting/methodology and consolidation changes, not necessarily less abuse). NCMEC reported a sharp rise in generative-AI-related CSAM reports — on the order of ~4,700 GAI-related reports in 2023 rising to ~67,000+ in 2024 (confirm exact figures). The Child Victim Identification Program (CVIP) catalogs known victims; survivors identified through CVIP can register to receive Victim Notifications whenever their imagery is identified in a new federal case, which is the gateway to seeking restitution. Document the dual path: report.cybertip.org (to report) vs. the victim-notification/restitution path (for identified survivors). Online enticement/sextortion is among the fastest-growing report categories.

entities.name: RAINN (Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network) — National Sexual Assault Hotline
entities.covers: Largest US anti-sexual-violence organization; operates the National Sexual Assault Hotline providing free, confidential 24/7 support, including for survivors of online and image-based abuse.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: National Sexual Assault Hotline: 1-800-656-HOPE (4673), plus online chat at online.rainn.org, free and confidential 24/7, routing callers to local affiliate service providers. RAINN also operates the DoD Safe Helpline and provides resources on technology-facilitated sexual abuse, sextortion, and image-based abuse. For a CSAM/IBSA survivor page, RAINN is the trauma-support and crisis backbone (emotional support, local referrals) to pair with the technical takedown tools — document the number, the chat option, and that it serves survivors of online/image-based abuse, not only physical assault.

entities.name: Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) — Report Remove (UK)
entities.covers: UK service (IWF with Childline/NSPCC) enabling under-18s to report nude/sexual images of themselves for removal from the internet; IWF also operates a public reporting hotline for CSAM.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Report Remove (run jointly by the Internet Watch Foundation and Childline/NSPCC) lets a young person under 18 in the UK confidentially report a sexual image/video of themselves; IWF assesses it and works to have it removed and hash-blocked across the industry, with Childline providing emotional support throughout. IWF is one of the world's leading CSAM hotlines and hash-list providers — it processed and actioned hundreds of thousands of reports in 2023, with self-generated imagery making up the large majority of the CSAM webpages it confirms. Document Report Remove as the leading UK/international youth self-report takedown path (complement to NCMEC Take It Down for US users), and IWF's hotline (report.iwf.org.uk) for the public to report CSAM URLs.

entities.name: Thorn (survivor-perspectives research)
entities.covers: Technology nonprofit building tools to defend children from sexual abuse; publishes research including survivor perspectives on the lifelong harm of CSAM recirculation.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Thorn's research is a citable source for the survivor-impact framing: that for survivors of recorded child sexual abuse, the permanence and ongoing redistribution of imagery causes continuous, recurring trauma (the 'crime that never ends'). Thorn also publishes data on sextortion and youth-generated imagery (e.g., its 'Deepfake Nudes & Young People' and sextortion reports) useful for quantifying the scale of image-based abuse among minors. Use Thorn for survivor-centered statistics and the psychological-harm narrative on the for-victims page; cite the specific report and year. Thorn builds detection tools (Safer) used by platforms, but for this domain its value is the research and the survivor-voice content.

entities.name: SWGfL Revenge Porn Helpline (UK)
entities.covers: UK helpline for adults experiencing non-consensual sharing of intimate images; the operator behind StopNCII.org.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: The Revenge Porn Helpline (run by the charity SWGfL) supports adult victims of intimate image abuse in the UK, offering case work, content removal assistance, and emotional support, and reports very high content-removal success rates across thousands of cases. It is the operational home of StopNCII.org. Document it as the UK adult counterpart to CCRI's helpline and as evidence that dedicated NCII helplines exist internationally. For non-US adult victims, this plus StopNCII is the primary route.

Most survivors don't know money recovery is possible.

Complements ai-csam-response and for-victims with a concrete enforceable right.
