findings.highest_value_gap: A single, authoritative, decision-tree TAKEDOWN GUIDE that routes each type of victim to the correct removal tool and walks the exact steps. The most citable, life-changing facts in this domain are operational — that Take It Down (under-18) and StopNCII (adults, incl. deepfakes) both work WITHOUT uploading the image (only an on-device hash is shared), that the 2025 TAKE IT DOWN Act now guarantees a 48-hour platform-removal right enforced by the FTC, and that survivors of known CSAM series can get DOJ restitution ($150k statutory minimum under Masha's Law, or a ~$35k one-time AVAA payment). Our existing for-victims/report-csam pages likely name some orgs, but the high-value gap is the concrete, current (2025), step-by-step \"how to actually get it taken down and recover damages\" path with exact tools, eligibility, phone numbers, and legal rights.

entities.name: National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) — CyberTipline
entities.covers: The congressionally designated US clearinghouse for reports of online child sexual exploitation; receives all 18 U.S.C. 2258A reports from electronic service providers and publishes the annual CyberTipline statistics that anchor the entire field.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: HEADLINE VOLUMES (cite the year explicitly): 2023 = 36.2 million reports (record high); 2024 = 20.5 million reports containing ~62.9 million files — a 43% DROP from 2023, which NCMEC attributes largely to new report 'bundling' of viral duplicates and to Meta's expansion of end-to-end encryption (adjusted for incidents, 2024 = 29.2 million distinct incidents); 2025 = 21.3 million reports / ~61.8 million files (NCMEC 'first look' 2026 blog). GENERATIVE AI: GAI-related reports rose 1,325%, from 4,700 in 2023 to 67,000 in 2024 (missingkids.org/blog/2025/ncmec-releases-new-data-2024-in-numbers); in 2025 GAI-nexus reports hit ~1.5 million, though ~1.1M were Amazon AI-Services dataset-scan submissions lacking offender/victim data — excluding those, 182,000+ reports involved offenders possessing/generating GAI CSAM. ONLINE ENTICEMENT (incl. sextortion): 546,000+ reports in 2024, a 192% jump over 2023; ~1.4 million in 2025. CHILD SEX TRAFFICKING reports: 26,823 in 2024 (+55% YoY), driven by REPORT Act mandatory reporting. 84% of 2024 reports resolved to locations outside the US. CAUTION: the YoY headline drop is a reporting-mechanics artifact, NOT a decline in abuse — always state this caveat. Verify the latest figures against the live CyberTipline data page since totals refresh annually.

entities.name: Internet Watch Foundation (IWF)
entities.covers: UK-based hotline and the leading global authority on assessing and removing child sexual abuse imagery from the open web; the primary independent source on AI-generated CSAM trends and severity.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: 2024 ANNUAL DATA & INSIGHTS REPORT: IWF assessed 424,000+ reports and confirmed CSAM (or links to it) a record 291,273 times; 91% of confirmed material was 'self-generated.' AI-GENERATED CSAM: 245 reports in 2024 contained actionable AI CSAM that broke UK law — a 380% rise from 51 in 2023 — equating to 7,644 images plus a small number of (first realistic) AI videos; ~39-40% of AI material was rated Category A (most severe: rape/sexual torture/bestiality), up sharply, and 193 of the 245 reports contained images that looked photorealistic. 62% of all CSAM webpages IWF found in 2024 were hosted in the EU. Earlier IWF research (Oct 2023) found 20,000+ AI images posted to one dark-web forum in a single month, ~3,000 depicting criminal child sexual abuse. The 2025 report shows continued escalation (Category A now the majority of illegal AI material). Cite the specific report year. NOTE: a major site redesign means the canonical landing is /annual-data-insights-report-2024/.

entities.name: FBI / Homeland Security Investigations / NCMEC — financial sextortion alerts
entities.covers: Joint US law-enforcement public-safety alerts on the explosive post-2021 rise of FINANCIAL sextortion targeting minors, overwhelmingly teenage boys.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: MOST ACTIONABLE STAT SET IN THE DOMAIN. FBI + HSI: 13,000+ reports of online financial sextortion of minors Oct 2021-Mar 2023, involving at least 12,600 victims (primarily boys) and linked to at least 20 suicides; a 20%+ YoY increase in the Oct 2022-Mar 2023 window. NCMEC CyberTipline financial-sextortion reports: 10,731 in 2022 → 26,718 in 2023 (nearly 100/day); NCMEC is aware of at least 36 teenage boys who died by suicide tied to sextortion since 2021. DEMOGRAPHICS: ~90% of financial-sextortion victims are boys aged 14-17 (Thorn/NCMEC analysis). Offenders are frequently organized groups based in West Africa ('Yahoo Boys') and Southeast Asia; Instagram and Snapchat are the most common contact platforms. Key actions to publish: don't pay, don't go silent, preserve evidence, report to NCMEC's CyberTipline and use Take It Down. Strong fit for for-parents, for-victims, and a dedicated financial-sextortion page.

entities.name: Thorn
entities.covers: Technology nonprofit building CSAM-detection tools (Safer) and publishing primary research on sextortion, self-generated imagery, and the generative-AI CSAM threat.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Thorn's 'Trends in Financial Sextortion' analysis of NCMEC data established the 90%-male-victim, 14-17 age profile and Instagram/Snapchat targeting. Thorn co-led the 2024 'Safety by Design for Generative AI' initiative with All Tech Is Human, securing public commitments from OpenAI, Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon, Anthropic, Stability AI, Civitai and others to prevent their models from producing CSAM (prevent training on CSAM, stress-test models, responsibly source datasets). Also publishes 'Youth Perspectives' / minors' self-generated-imagery surveys. Best citable anchor for the 'Safety by Design' and industry-response framing on the ai-csam-response page.

entities.name: Stanford Internet Observatory
entities.covers: Academic center that produced two field-shaping investigations: CSAM contamination in AI training data, and structural strain on the NCMEC CyberTipline reporting pipeline.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Dec 2023 report (David Thiel) found 1,000+ instances of known CSAM in the LAION-5B dataset used to train Stable Diffusion and other image generators, prompting LAION takedown/retraining — the empirical basis for 'AI image models learned partly from real abuse imagery.' 2024 report 'The CyberTipline: A Vital Resource Under Strain' documented that the pipeline is overwhelmed by volume, that legal ambiguity (the lack of an affirmative search duty) limits proactive detection, and that many reports lack actionable detail — core evidence for the reform debate (REPORT Act, EARN IT). NOTE: SIO was substantially wound down/restructured in 2024-2025, so cite the archived PDFs directly rather than expecting an active program.

entities.name: TAKE IT DOWN Act (Public Law 119-12)
entities.covers: Landmark US federal law criminalizing nonconsensual intimate imagery — including AI-generated deepfakes — of adults and minors, and mandating fast platform takedowns.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Full name: 'Tools to Address Known Exploitation by Immobilizing Technological Deepfakes on Websites and Networks Act.' Sponsors Sens. Ted Cruz (R-TX) and Amy Klobuchar (D-MN); House champion Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar. Senate passed Feb 13, 2025 (unanimous); House passed Apr 28, 2025 (409-2); SIGNED BY PRESIDENT TRUMP MAY 19, 2025. Criminalizes knowingly publishing nonconsensual intimate images — real OR AI-generated/deepfake — of identifiable adults and minors (harsher penalties for minors). Requires 'covered platforms' to build a notice-and-removal process and remove flagged NCII (and known copies) within 48 HOURS of a valid request; platform-compliance deadline is one year after enactment = MAY 19, 2026. Enforced by the FTC as an unfair/deceptive practice. NOTE for balance: EFF and other civil-liberties groups warn the takedown mechanism could be abused and pressure platforms to over-remove or weaken encryption. This is the single most important NEW enacted US statute in the domain — belongs prominently on report-csam, for-victims, for-compliance-teams.

entities.name: 18 U.S.C. § 2258A (mandatory provider reporting) + REPORT Act (Public Law 118-59)
entities.covers: The core US statute requiring electronic service providers to report apparent CSAM to NCMEC's CyberTipline, as significantly amended by the 2024 REPORT Act.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Baseline 2258A: US providers must report apparent CSAM to NCMEC, but there is NO general affirmative duty to monitor or affirmatively search for it (a critical legal nuance often misunderstood). REPORT ACT ('Revising Existing Procedures On Reporting via Technology Act,' PL 118-59) passed the House Apr 29, 2024 and was SIGNED MAY 7, 2024. It: (1) expanded mandatory reporting to explicitly include child sex TRAFFICKING and online ENTICEMENT/coercion (previously not required), (2) extended the data-PRESERVATION period for reported content from 90 days to ONE YEAR, and (3) raised failure-to-report penalties (up to $850,000 first offense / $1,000,000 subsequent for providers with 100M+ MAUs). NCMEC issued trafficking/enticement identifier guidance in Oct 2024. This statutory framework is why the NCMEC numbers exist and explains the 2024 spikes in enticement (+192%) and trafficking (+55%) reports. Explain on report-csam, for-tech-ceos, for-compliance-teams, for-developers.

entities.name: EARN IT Act (Eliminating Abusive and Rampant Neglect of Interactive Technologies Act)
entities.covers: Recurring US bill that would narrow Section 230 immunity for CSAM and create a national commission — repeatedly advanced in committee but NEVER enacted.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Reintroduced as S.1207 by Sens. Graham and Blumenthal in April 2023; UNANIMOUSLY advanced out of the Senate Judiciary Committee on May 11, 2023 — but, as in 2020 and 2022, it never received a full Senate vote and DID NOT become law; it was not reintroduced in the 119th Congress (2025-26). Would remove Section 230 immunity for state CSAM civil/criminal claims and create a 19-member National Commission on Online Child Sexual Exploitation Prevention to issue voluntary best practices. Strongly opposed by EFF, CDT, and security experts who argue it endangers end-to-end encryption. IMPORTANT framing: present accurately as PROPOSED-BUT-NOT-ENACTED, in contrast to the REPORT Act and TAKE IT DOWN Act which DID pass — this is the field's most common point of public confusion.

entities.name: EU Regulation to Prevent and Combat Child Sexual Abuse (CSA Regulation / 'Chat Control')
entities.covers: Proposed EU regulation to require online services to detect, report, and remove CSAM and grooming — the most contested digital-rights fight in the EU, still not final law.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Proposed by the European Commission May 2022. The flashpoint is 'detection orders' that critics call 'chat control' because they could compel scanning of private/encrypted messages (client-side scanning). It stalled for years; SEVEN successive Council presidencies failed to reach a deal. KEY 2025 DEVELOPMENTS: an Oct 14, 2025 vote collapsed after Germany signaled opposition; on Oct 31, 2025 the Danish Presidency dropped MANDATORY detection orders, converting scanning to VOLUNTARY plus risk-mitigation/age-verification duties; on Nov 26, 2025 COREPER/Council adopted a (partial) general-approach negotiating mandate in a close vote, sending it to TRILOGUE with the Parliament and Commission (ongoing into 2026, with no agreed location yet for the proposed new EU Centre on Child Sexual Abuse). Meanwhile an interim regulation permitting VOLUNTARY detection by providers was extended (to April 2026) to avoid a legal gap. Present as ACTIVE, UNRESOLVED — not settled law — and verify trilogue status at publication. EFF/EDRi track the opposition; IWF backs closing the detection gap.

entities.name: EU Digital Services Act (DSA)
entities.covers: EU-wide platform-governance law imposing illegal-content removal, systemic-risk-assessment, and transparency duties — the live, enforceable EU baseline while the dedicated CSA Regulation remains stalled.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Very Large Online Platforms/Search Engines (45M+ EU users) came under direct Commission supervision from Aug 25, 2023; the DSA applies to all in-scope services since FEB 17, 2024. Requires rapid removal of illegal content (including CSAM) upon notice, annual systemic-risk assessment and mitigation that EXPLICITLY includes risks to minors and fundamental rights, trusted-flagger mechanisms, and transparency reporting. Penalties up to 6% of global annual turnover. Useful distinction for for-compliance-teams/for-tech-ceos: the DSA is enforceable NOW, whereas the CSA Regulation is still in negotiation.

entities.name: UK Online Safety Act 2023 (enforced by Ofcom)
entities.covers: UK law imposing legal duties of care on user-to-user and search services, with CSAM/grooming as 'priority illegal content,' enforced by regulator Ofcom.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Royal Assent Oct 26, 2023. PHASED ENFORCEMENT: illegal-content duties became enforceable MAR 17, 2025 (services had to complete illegal-harms risk assessments and apply Ofcom's codes); Ofcom published its Protection of Children Codes Apr 24, 2025; children's risk assessments were due Jul 24, 2025 and child-safety duties plus 'highly effective age assurance' / age verification for pornography and other harmful content took effect JUL 25, 2025. CSAM and grooming require proactive measures. PENALTIES: up to £18 million OR 10% of global annual turnover (whichever is greater); business disruption/blocking measures and senior-manager criminal liability in extreme cases. Ofcom opened enforcement programmes targeting CSAM on file-sharing services and issued its first OSA fine (£1m+) in late 2025. Highly relevant to for-compliance-teams, for-tech-ceos, international-resources, and the age-assurance debate.

entities.name: Australia eSafety Commissioner
entities.covers: World-first national online safety regulator with takedown, mandatory industry-code, and Basic Online Safety Expectations powers covering CSAM ('class 1' material) — and the world's first under-16 social-media ban.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Operates under the Online Safety Act 2021. Phase 1/2 industry codes and standards: Phase 2 Age-Restricted Material Codes registered Jun 27, 2025 (effective Dec 27, 2025); six further Phase 2 codes registered Sep 9, 2025 (effective Mar 9, 2026) covering app stores, social media core + messaging, RES and designated internet services — requiring age assurance to keep children from pornography, high-impact violence, and self-harm/eating-disorder content. Earlier enforceable standards for relevant electronic services and designated internet services took effect Dec 22, 2024. Civil penalties up to AUD 49.5 million for breaching a direction. SEPARATELY, the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act bans under-16s from specified platforms, with enforcement from DEC 10, 2025 — a globally watched precedent. eSafety also has CSAM and image-based-abuse takedown powers and issues transparency reporting notices to major platforms. Strong fit for international-resources and the age-assurance discussion.

entities.name: WeProtect Global Alliance
entities.covers: Global multi-stakeholder alliance (governments, companies, civil society) coordinating the response to online child sexual exploitation; publishes the biennial Global Threat Assessment — the single best international synthesis citation.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: Its Global Threat Assessment 2023 reported an 87% increase in confirmed CSAM reports since 2019 (to 32+ million reports in 2022) and flagged generative AI, financial sextortion, and self-generated content as the fastest-accelerating threats. Best one-citation answer to 'what is the global scale of the problem.' A 2025/2026 edition may now exist — check for the latest before publishing.

entities.name: INHOPE — global hotline network
entities.covers: The global network of CSAM-reporting hotlines (50+ countries) coordinating cross-border notice-and-takedown via the ICCAM classification platform.
entities.knowledge_to_fold_in: INHOPE routes reporters to their national hotline and operates the ICCAM system member hotlines use to classify and exchange CSAM reports internationally so material can be taken down in the host country. The right answer to 'how do I report CSAM outside the US/UK' — a natural addition to report-csam and international-resources.

synthesis.executive_summary:
CORRECTED AFTER LIVE-CORPUS INSPECTION. digitalharm.org is already a strong, mature, well-sourced resource, not a thin scaffold — so the job is targeted gap-closing and consolidation, not a rebuild. Verified reality: the real content is an 8-chapter report in content/locales/en/report.ts (2,031 lines: exposure, addiction, escalation, ai-generated, interventions, technology, prevention, recommendations) with 347 external links across 50+ primary/first-tier domains (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, iwf.org.uk, c3p/protectchildren.ca, thorn.org, missingkids.org, law.cornell.edu, eur-lex, etc.); the /citations page auto-extracts 259 citations; there are 9 audience guides (/for-victims, /for-parents, /for-educators, /for-offenders, /for-therapists, /for-attorneys, /for-tech-ceos, /for-developers, /for-compliance-teams) plus /for-reporting (114 platforms), /apps, /tools, /get-help (+bay-area), /about, /browse, /search. Critically, several things I would otherwise flag as gaps already exist and are good: SEARCH is well-built (lib/search.ts, 318 lines, with exact-phrase boosting, a synonym/keyword recall layer, per-section indexing that feeds /sitemap.ts, a persistent header search box, and a /browse topic map); the NCMEC 2024 'bundling' artifact is already explained in a dedicated 'Reading the numbers' section; the Stanford/Pfefferkorn ambiguous-'Generative AI'-category caveat is already stated on /about and in the AI chapter; PhotoDNA and the KNOWN-vs-NOVEL detection distinction are covered in depth; the encryption / Chat Control / EARN IT / Apple-NeuralHash / Amy v. Apple debate is deep and current; Grubbs and moral incongruence ARE present (the ICD-11 moral-judgment exclusion is cited to Grubbs 2020); PhotoDNA appears 64 times and Phoenix 11 twelve times; and /for-offenders already routes to Troubled Desire and Stop It Now with an honest US/UK/Germany confidentiality discussion. PLAN.md confirms every planned wave through v2.0 has shipped, including a platform-accountability scorecard guarded by a CI lint (scripts/check-perishable-citations.ts) that fails the build if a named individual lacks a co-occurring citation. This is a serious resource.

The genuinely remaining, confirmed-by-query gaps are concentrated and high-leverage. FIRST and most important for credibility: the contested porn-science is real-but-unbalanced. The pro-model and skeptic camps are under-named — Prause = 0, Kraus = 0, AASECT = 0, Ferguson = 0, I-PACE = 0, Carnes = 0, Grubbs = 1, Voon = 2 — so the addiction chapter currently leans toward the harm/addiction framing without the named counter-voices (Prause's LPP findings, Ley/Prause/Finn 'Emperor Has No Clothes,' Ferguson & Hartley on the weak porn-aggression link, AASECT's 2016 position) that make the treatment honestly even-handed rather than reading as anti-porn — a real risk given the 'Digital Harm' title. SECOND, demand-side/perpetration-prevention skews UK/Germany (Dunkelfeld and Troubled Desire are well covered at 17 and 24 mentions) but the US flagship (Johns Hopkins Moore Center 'Help Wanted,' Letourneau) and Finland's ReDirection are absent (0 each), and the honest 'does treatment actually work?' counterweight is thin (Mokros = 1, Holper = 0) despite being the intellectual-honesty differentiator. THIRD, two top-tier sources are missing: Childlight's 'Into the Light Index' (~302M children/year, 2024) = 0, and Common Sense Media's gold-standard youth-exposure data = 1. FOURTH, despite excellent per-topic depth, there is no single CONSOLIDATED, durable reference that journalists/policymakers can deep-link: no who's-who ORGANIZATION DIRECTORY mapped by function (the orgs are cited across chapters but never assembled), no standalone dated STATISTICS sheet (the numbers are scattered across chapters), and no status-aware LAWS tracker that cleanly separates ENACTED law (TAKE IT DOWN Act, REPORT Act, 2258A, EU DSA, UK OSA, Australia OSA) from PROPOSED/stalled bills (EARN IT, EU CSA Regulation). FIFTH, smaller fixes: survivor restitution remedies are thin (Masha 2, §2255 1, Victims Reserve 1); ECPAT Luxembourg terminology could be made explicit; and the README is stale (it documents a /sources route that does not exist — the page is /citations — and a Feb-2026 review date contradicted by PLAN.md's May 2026). The work sequences as a v0.5 balance-and-accuracy pass (name the porn-science skeptic + pro-model camps; deepen moral incongruence; reconcile the README), a v1.0 authority-consolidation wave (org directory, dated stats sheet, enacted-vs-proposed laws tracker, expanded editorial-standards/COI page), a v1.5 depth wave (US/Finland demand-side + honest-limitations; restitution remedies; by-country reporting; Childlight/Common Sense numbers), and a v2.0 differentiation wave (neutral tool/curricula comparisons, ECPAT terminology authority, living-tracker re-verification cadence). Every statistic should be re-verified against each org's latest figures before publishing.
top_competitors: NCMEC / missingkids.org — authoritative and the canonical reporting/removal home (CyberTipline, Take It Down), but fragmented and US-operational, not a teaching resource. We already cite it heavily (189 mentions across content) and link it; beat it by adding the one thing it lacks — a consolidated who's-who ORG DIRECTORY and the synthesis layer — while always linking it by name as the canonical action.

Internet Watch Foundation (iwf.org.uk) — the best CSAM threat-data and AI-CSAM authority, but UK-centric and data-dense. We cite it well (74 mentions, 14 links); beat it on synthesis by consolidating its hard numbers (291,273 webpages in 2024; 245 AI-CSAM reports, +380%; ~40% Category A) into a single dated stats sheet that also explains the webpages-vs-reports methodology difference between IWF and NCMEC — a trust signal no one surfaces.

Fight the New Drug (fightthenewdrug.org) — huge reach and slick 'porn is harmful' content, repeatedly criticized for cherry-picking and downplayed LDS ties despite a 'non-religious' claim. Beat it on the SAME topics with balanced, peer-reviewed evidence and explicit acknowledgement of contested claims. This is precisely where our addiction chapter must name the skeptics (Prause, Ley, Ferguson, AASECT) — currently absent — so we are visibly even-handed where they are not.

Covenant Eyes 'Porn Stats' (covenanteyes.com) — one of the most-cited AND most-misleading stat compilations online (outdated, decontextualized, untraceable figures; undisclosed accountability-software + Christian agenda). Beat it by out-ranking it with a single consolidated, rigorously dated, named-source, myth-busting statistics page that corrects the numbers it put into circulation; we have the citations scattered across chapters but not yet the one corrective stat sheet.

Your Brain on Porn (yourbrainonporn.com) + NoFap communities — originated the viral 'rewire/reboot' narrative with enormous reach, but the founder was not a credentialed neuroscientist and the claims are widely disputed. Beat them by honestly adjudicating which claims (dopamine, sensitization, 'reboot,' 'flatline') have real support vs are extrapolated from substance-addiction analogies, citing skeptics (Ley already at 8 mentions; add Prause) and supporters (Brand at 5; add I-PACE framing, Voon) by name.

Lucy Faithfull Foundation / Stop It Now UK (stopitnow.org.uk) — the world's leading perpetration-prevention helpline; the standard we must match and globalize. We cover the UK/Germany demand-side well (Troubled Desire 24, Dunkelfeld 17, Stop It Now 9) but are missing the US flagship (Moore Center 'Help Wanted'/Letourneau, 0) and Finland's ReDirection (0); beat the field by being the ONE place that maps confidential 'get help before you harm' routes across the US, UK, Germany, and Finland with the honest limitations of each.

General parent-safety incumbents (Common Sense Media, Internet Matters, Protect Young Eyes, Bark) — strong on age-based advice and how-to control setup. Beat them by owning the 'why / what's the evidence' layer and porn-and-exploitation specificity; note Common Sense Media's gold-standard youth-exposure data is barely cited on our site (1 mention) and should anchor the exposure chapter, /for-parents, and /for-educators.
must_fold_in: The porn-science SKEPTIC camp, by name, for balance (currently absent: Prause 0, Kraus 0, AASECT 0, Ferguson 0): Prause et al. (2015, Biological Psychology) — problem users showed LOWER LPP to sexual cues than controls, opposite of drug cue-reactivity; Steele/Prause (2013) — P300 tracked desire not hypersexuality; Ley, Prause & Finn (2014) 'The Emperor Has No Clothes' (Current Sexual Health Reports); Ferguson & Hartley (2022) — the porn-aggression link is weak/possibly artifactual; AASECT 2016 position (exact language) — insufficient empirical evidence to classify sex/porn addiction as a disorder. These are the named counter-voices our addiction chapter needs to be visibly even-handed.

The pro-model camp, named and balanced against the skeptics (thin today: Brand 5, Voon 2, I-PACE 0): Brand et al. (2016/2019) I-PACE model as the dominant behavioral-addiction framework; Voon et al. (2014, PLoS ONE) cue-reactivity fMRI (with Voon's own caveat that it does not prove porn is 'addictive'); Wright's meta-analyses on satisfaction (2017) and aggression (2016); Kraus, Voon & Potenza (2016) centrist 'evidence-gaps-preclude-addiction-classification' position. Pair explicitly with the skeptics so both poles are represented.

Deepen Grubbs's moral-incongruence model from a single passing mention to a real anchor (Grubbs = 1 today): Grubbs, Perry, Wilt & Reid (2019), Archives of Sexual Behavior 48(2):397-415 — the PPMI two-pathway model and the religiosity/shame finding that self-perceived 'porn addiction' often tracks moral disapproval more than frequency of use. This is the field's load-bearing concept and currently under-weighted relative to its importance.

The US + Finland demand-side programs that close the geographic gap (Moore Center 0, Letourneau 0, Help Wanted 0, ReDirection 0 today): Johns Hopkins Moore Center 'Help Wanted' (Elizabeth Letourneau; anonymous online prevention course; RCT NCT06300957 underway; 'attraction does not doom a person to offend'); Protect Children ReDirection (Finland) — 26,000+ anonymous dark-web CSAM-user survey responses, self-help program opened 70,000+ times, 74% reported reduced/ceased use, only ~3% of users who want help actually get it (Insoll et al., Journal of Online Trust and Safety, 2022 & 2024).

The honest 'does prevention treatment work?' evidence (thin today: Mokros 1, Holper 0): Mokros & Banse (2019, J Sex Med) found NO demonstrated treatment-specific reduction in proneness to offend in the Dunkelfeld data; Holper et al. (2024) — risk-focused treatment can INCREASE recidivism in LOW-risk individuals; the 2024 Dunkelfeld registry follow-up + König (2025) iatrogenic-effects debate vs Beier's rebuttal; UK MoJ SOTP (Mews 2017) associated with slightly higher reoffending. No RCT-grade proof that treatment reduces offending yet exists — stating this is the intellectual-honesty differentiator.

Childlight 'Into the Light Index' (2024, University of Edinburgh) — the NEWEST authoritative global-prevalence figure and currently uncited (0 mentions): ~302 million children (1 in 8, 12.6%) were victims of online sexual abuse/exposure in the prior 12 months; framed as a global health pandemic; corroborated by UNSW and the Guardian. Highly quotable; cite precisely with the 2024 year and Childlight as source to anchor the global-scale framing.

Common Sense Media 'Teens and Pornography' (2022/2023) — the gold-standard US youth-exposure source, barely cited (1 mention): avg first exposure ~12; 15% by age 10; 54% by 13; 73% have seen porn; 58% accidental; 41% saw porn during the school day (44% on school devices); 52% have seen violent/aggressive depictions. Should anchor the exposure chapter, /for-parents, and the phone-free-school argument in /for-educators. Pair with Dickenson, Coleman et al. (2018, JAMA Network Open) — 8.6% clinically relevant distress (10.3% men / 7.0% women).

US survivor restitution remedies most survivors don't know exist (thin today: Masha 2, §2255 1, Victims Reserve 1): 18 U.S.C. § 2255 ('Masha's Law,' AVAA 2018) — $150,000 statutory minimum civil damages per defendant; Paroline v. United States, 572 U.S. 434 (2014) — proximate-cause restitution (already partly present at 5 mentions); AVAA $3,000 minimum trafficking restitution + the DOJ Child Pornography Victims Reserve 'defined monetary assistance' (~$35,000 one-time, inflation-adjusted) via NCMEC's Child Victim Identification Program. Marsh Law / Carol Hepburn are the practitioner anchors for /for-attorneys and /for-victims.

The full WeProtect / ECPAT / INHOPE / INTERPOL global-architecture facts for a consolidated org directory and by-country reporting (cited in passing but not assembled): WeProtect Global Threat Assessment (87% rise in CSAM reports since 2019; 32M+ in 2022); ECPAT Disrupting Harm + the Luxembourg Guidelines terminology authority (Luxembourg present at 3 mentions — make it the explicit basis for 'CSAM not child pornography'); INHOPE (55 hotlines/51 countries; 1.4-day in-network vs 41-day out-of-network removal); INTERPOL ICSE (38,825 victims identified by Mar 2024 to 56,000+ by Sept 2025); Tech Coalition Lantern (launched Nov 2023; present at 2 mentions).

The Thorn/All Tech Is Human 'Safety by Design for Generative AI' framework (April 2024), named explicitly — the single most citable industry standard for AI labs, signed by Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Stability AI, Civitai, Mistral and others, with a 2025 progress report. Thorn is already at 42 mentions and Stanford's LAION-5B finding is present — ensure the Safety-by-Design framework and signatory list specifically anchor /for-developers and /for-tech-ceos as the actionable standard, alongside the LAION-5B/Re-LAION dataset-integrity story already covered.

The full detection-infrastructure signal-sharing rails for the existing 'how detection works' depth (PhotoDNA already at 64 mentions; rails thinner): name the KNOWN-vs-NOVEL distinction (already covered) plus the cross-platform signal-sharing layer — NCMEC hash-sharing (covered), Tech Coalition Lantern (2 mentions), INHOPE ICCAM, INTERPOL ICSE, and Meta's open-sourced PDQ/TMK+PDQF (2019) — so the detection story explains not just hashing but how an offender pushed off one platform is caught on the next, with the collision-attack and client-side-scanning/E2EE tradeoffs already well covered.

ECPAT Luxembourg Guidelines as the explicit terminology authority feeding a glossary/terminology section: WHY to say 'child sexual abuse material' not 'child pornography' (the latter implies a legitimacy/consent that cannot exist for a child), with precise survivor-centered definitions of grooming, sextortion, self-generated content, capping, and live-streamed abuse — currently referenced (3 mentions) but not assembled into the canonical terminology reference the site could own.
